The platform includes a digital guidebook, upsell tools that present add-ons at the right moment, and integration with property management systems. For hoteliers and vacation rental managers, this reduces repetitive messages and brings extra revenue per booking.

item.title: Edge Impulse
item.description:
Edge Impulse brings machine learning to small devices. An engineer collects data from sensors such as accelerometers, microphones, and cameras, labels it, designs a processing pipeline, trains a model in the browser, and exports an optimized version that runs on a microcontroller or edge processor. Applications include detecting equipment faults, recognizing keywords, and spotting objects.

The platform supports a wide range of hardware and shows estimates of memory use and latency before deployment, which matters when resources are tiny. Tools help with data collection and testing, and integrations connect to major chip vendors. Qualcomm acquired the company to strengthen its edge AI offering.

item.title: Esko
item.description:
Esko serves the packaging and label industries. Designers use ArtiosCAD to create the structural design of boxes and cartons, with dielines that show cuts and folds. ArtPro+ and related tools prepare artwork for printing, handling color, trapping, and layout across the many steps between a design and the press.

Workflow tools automate preparation and approval. Software checks files for errors, compares versions, and routes proofs, which reduces mistakes in printed packaging where a typo can mean a costly reprint. Cloud platforms support collaboration between brands, designers, and printers, and AI helps with checking and automating routine tasks.

item.title: Everlaw
item.description:
Everlaw helps legal teams work through evidence. Documents are uploaded, processed, and made searchable, and reviewers tag them, share notes, and build case narratives. Visual tools show relationships and timelines, and cloud delivery means teams can collaborate without installing software.

AI speeds up the work. Predictive coding ranks documents by likely relevance, clustering groups similar content, and generative features summarize documents, answer questions across a set, and draft deposition outlines. Everlaw has tools used by public interest lawyers and human rights investigators, and the company supports access programs.

item.title: Eyenuk
item.description:
Eyenuk focuses on automated eye screening. A technician captures retinal images with a compatible camera, and EyeArt analyzes them and reports whether signs of more-than-mild disease are present, flagging patients who need referral. The process takes about a minute and does not need a specialist to read the images.

The purpose is to expand screening for people with diabetes who miss annual eye exams. Primary care clinics, endocrinology practices, and optometrists use it to catch disease earlier. The company has expanded the technology to other conditions and offers versions for different clinical settings.

item.title: FiscalNote
item.description:
FiscalNote is a policy intelligence platform. Government relations and compliance teams set up alerts for topics they care about, and the system monitors legislation, regulatory dockets, and court cases in many jurisdictions, notifying them when something changes. This replaces manual tracking of dozens of websites.

AI summarizes long documents, estimates which bills are likely to move, and helps teams assess the impact on their organization. The platform also supports collaboration, so teams can share notes, assign tasks, and report to executives. Related products cover policy research and the news in a field.

item.title: Floify
item.description:
Floify handles the document stage of mortgage lending. Loan officers invite borrowers to a secure portal where they upload pay stubs, bank statements, and other items, sign disclosures electronically, and watch the status of their loan. The portal carries the lender’s branding.

Automation reduces manual follow-up. The system sends reminders for missing documents, sorts and labels uploads, and updates borrowers and real estate agents as milestones are reached. It connects to loan origination systems so data moves between them. Analytics show where loans get stuck.

item.title: ForeFlight
item.description:
ForeFlight is an app for planning and flying. Pilots build routes, check weather and airspace, file flight plans, and view approach plates and charts. In the air, it shows moving maps and traffic and weather from compatible receivers, which replaces paper charts.

Weather is a big part. Layers show forecasts, radar, and hazards, and tools highlight conditions most likely to affect a given route. Performance and weight and balance planning help with safety, and integrations connect to avionics and tablets. Teams in flight departments use it to share data.

item.title: FourKites
item.description:
FourKites is a supply chain visibility platform. It collects location and status data from carriers, telematics devices, and ocean and air sources, and shows shippers where each load is. Predictive estimates of arrival time account for traffic, weather, and dwell time at facilities, which are more accurate than static schedules.

Alerts warn teams of delays so they can reroute or notify customers. Yard and dock scheduling tools coordinate appointments, and analytics help identify problem carriers or lanes. AI agents handle tasks like checking on late shipments and communicating with carriers.

item.title: Freed
item.description:
Freed helps clinicians finish notes faster. During a visit, with patient consent, it records the conversation and produces a structured note in a familiar format, which the clinician reviews, edits, and copies into the record. It also drafts instructions for the patient.

It is popular with independent practitioners, such as physicians, nurse practitioners, and therapists, because it is easy to set up and priced for individuals. Features include templates by specialty, custom note styles, and a learning feature that adapts to how a clinician writes.

item.title: Glass Health
item.description:
Glass Health helps with clinical reasoning and documentation. A clinician enters or dictates a patient summary, and the assistant proposes a list of possible diagnoses, along with reasoning and suggested next steps. A plan builder drafts assessment and plan sections, and reference citations let the user check where claims come from.

It also supports note writing, and a library of clinical guidelines and content supports decisions. Physicians, residents, and students use it to think through cases and save time on write-ups. The product emphasizes that the clinician stays responsible for decisions.

item.title: Greenlight Guru
item.description:
Greenlight Guru serves a heavily regulated industry. Medical device makers must document how a product was designed, how risks were assessed, and how problems are corrected. The platform organizes these records, links requirements to risks and tests, and keeps them audit ready, replacing documents scattered in shared drives.

Modules cover design controls, risk management, document control, training, supplier management, and corrective and preventive actions. AI features help draft documents and risk analyses and answer questions about regulations, saving time on repetitive writing. A clinical module supports post-market work.

item.title: Gusto
item.description:
Gusto is built for employers without a dedicated HR department. A business adds its team, and Gusto calculates pay, withholds and files payroll taxes, and pays employees and contractors. Employees get pay stubs and benefits information in an app, and onboarding checklists collect forms and agreements from new hires.

The platform extends beyond payroll. It offers health insurance and retirement plan administration through partners, time tracking, hiring tools, and compliance support such as reminders and labor law guidance. AI features help flag likely filing errors, draft job descriptions and policies, and answer HR questions in plain language.

item.title: Heuritech
item.description:
Heuritech applies computer vision to fashion trends. Its models scan images from social platforms and recognize garments, colors, prints, and shapes, then measure how frequently each appears and how quickly that is changing. The output is a forecast of which items will grow or fade in a market.

Brands use the forecasts to decide what to design, produce, and stock, which can reduce unsold inventory. Reports are segmented by region, age group, and category, and the platform includes tools for tracking competitors and monitoring product performance against trends.

item.title: Hippocratic AI
item.description:
Hippocratic AI focuses on non-diagnostic work in healthcare. Its agents call patients to check on recovery after discharge, remind them to take medication, prepare them for procedures, and monitor chronic conditions. The calls are long, patient conversations that clinical staff rarely have time to make.

Safety is the stated priority. The company tests its models with clinicians and designs the agents to stay within defined roles, escalating to a nurse or doctor when a patient reports symptoms that need attention. Health systems deploy them to extend staff capacity and reach patients between visits.

item.title: HiredScore
item.description:
HiredScore applies AI to the early stages of hiring. When applications arrive, it grades candidates against the requirements of the role, surfaces people who might be good fits, including past applicants and current employees, and helps recruiters focus on promising profiles first.

It integrates with applicant tracking systems and HR platforms, and Workday acquired the company to build AI into its talent products. Features include internal mobility recommendations, which help companies fill roles from within, and reporting to monitor process fairness and compliance.

item.title: Hunchly
item.description:
Hunchly is a browser extension for investigations. As a researcher browses, it saves each page as it appeared, with screenshots, timestamps, and hash values that help show the content has not been altered. Pages are organized into cases, so evidence from a long investigation stays together.

The tool adds notes, tags, and a way to search across captured content. Reports can be generated for sharing or for legal use. It is popular with open-source intelligence investigators, journalists, and fraud and law enforcement analysts who need to preserve content that may disappear.

item.title: Instrumentl
item.description:
Instrumentl is a grant discovery and management platform. A nonprofit describes its mission and programs, and the system recommends foundation and government grants that fit, with details on the funder’s giving history, typical award sizes, and past recipients. Alerts notify the team when new matches appear.

Once a grant is identified, a tracker handles tasks, deadlines, reports, and documents for each application, with collaboration for the team. AI assists with research, summarizing funder priorities and drafting parts of proposals, though grant writing still depends on strong program knowledge.

item.title: Jane
item.description:
Jane is practice management software for health and wellness clinics. Patients book online, receive reminders, and pay through the system, while practitioners chart visits, manage insurance billing, and run reports. A telehealth feature supports virtual visits.

The AI assistant helps with documentation. A clinician dictates or types notes, and Jane structures them into a SOAP note, saving time at the end of the day. Multi-practitioner clinics can manage schedules, rooms, and staff in one place.

item.title: Jobber
item.description:
Jobber is built for small service companies such as lawn care, cleaning, plumbing, and locksmith businesses. Owners send quotes, schedule jobs on a calendar, dispatch crews, and invoice customers, with a mobile app for the crew to see their route, take notes, and collect payment on site.

Client-facing features help win and keep work. Customers can request services online, approve quotes, pay invoices, and receive reminders and arrival notices, and a client hub keeps their history together. Automations send follow-ups and review requests. An AI assistant drafts messages and helps convert rough notes into a clear quote.

item.title: Kajabi
item.description:
Kajabi is an all-in-one platform for knowledge businesses. A creator builds a site, sells courses, memberships, coaching, and digital downloads, collects payments, runs email campaigns, and hosts a community, all from one dashboard instead of stitching together several tools.

Marketing and automation are built in. Landing pages, funnels, email sequences, and a pipeline for leads let creators sell without extra software. The AI assistant helps write copy, plan courses, and generate emails, and analytics show revenue and engagement. Mobile apps for members are available.

item.title: Keela
item.description:
Keela helps small and mid-sized nonprofits manage supporters. It keeps donor records, gifts, and communication history, processes online donations, runs email campaigns, and supports events and volunteer tracking. The platform aims to be affordable and approachable for teams without a dedicated data staff.

AI features guide outreach. Engagement scoring highlights supporters likely to give again or increase gifts, timing suggestions prompt contact when it is most effective, and a writing assistant drafts appeals and thank-you notes. Reports show campaign results and giving trends.

item.title: Kentik
item.description:
Kentik gives network teams insight into how traffic moves. It collects flow records, routing information, and metrics from routers, switches, and cloud networks, stores them at large scale, and lets engineers query who is talking to whom and how much. That helps with capacity planning, troubleshooting, and cost control.

Security and reliability uses include detecting DDoS attacks and unusual traffic patterns, analyzing BGP routing changes, and finding the reason for a slowdown across multiple networks. An AI assistant lets users ask questions in plain language and speeds up root cause analysis. Cloud and data center networks are covered.

item.title: LeanTaaS
item.description:
LeanTaaS builds software for healthcare capacity. Hospitals struggle with uneven demand: operating rooms sit idle while patients wait, infusion chairs are overbooked on some days, and beds are not available when needed. LeanTaaS forecasts demand and recommends schedules that balance resources and reduce wait times.

Its iQueue products cover operating rooms, infusion centers, and inpatient beds. Algorithms assess historical patterns and help staff adjust block time, appointment slots, and staffing. Improvements can increase the number of patients served without adding space.

item.title: Medidata
item.description:
Medidata is a major provider of clinical trial technology. Rave Electronic Data Capture collects patient data from trial sites, and other products handle randomization, imaging, patient-reported outcomes, and trial planning. Pharmaceutical companies and research organizations use the platform to run studies from start to finish.

AI and analytics help trial teams. Models flag sites with unusual data, predict enrollment problems, and help design studies using historical trial data, and the company has built synthetic control arm methods that use past patients to supplement studies. These aim to make trials faster and more efficient.

item.title: Medisafe
item.description:
Medisafe helps people take medicines as prescribed. Users enter their medications, get reminders at the right time, and log doses. If a dose is missed, the app follows up, and caregivers can be notified. Interaction checks warn about conflicts between drugs when a new one is added.

Programs with pharmacies, health plans, and drugmakers build on the app, offering support for particular conditions and tracking adherence. Features include refill reminders, health measurement tracking, and educational content. AI helps personalize reminders and detect patterns.

item.title: Mentalyc
item.description:
Mentalyc is an AI note-taking tool for mental health professionals. A therapist records a session, uploads audio, or enters brief notes, and the tool generates a structured progress note that matches the format their practice uses. The clinician edits and approves it.

The product emphasizes privacy, since therapy content is sensitive. It states that it follows health privacy rules and offers controls such as removing identifying details. It also supports treatment plans and can learn a therapist’s style over time.

item.title: Moveworks
item.description:
Moveworks brings an assistant to employee support. Workers ask for help in Slack, Teams, or a portal, and the system understands the request, finds the answer in company knowledge, or completes the action by connecting to IT and HR systems. Common examples are unlocking an account, requesting software, or finding a policy.

The company grew by focusing on large enterprises and on language understanding specific to workplace requests. It added generative AI and agent capabilities, with a platform for building custom agents and connecting to many business systems.

item.title: Muck Rack
item.description:
Muck Rack is a public relations platform. PR professionals search its database to find journalists who cover a topic, see what they have written recently, and build media lists. They send pitches and track responses, and the platform monitors news to show where their company or clients are mentioned.

Reporting tools measure coverage by reach and sentiment, and dashboards show how campaigns perform. AI features summarize articles, suggest journalists, and help draft pitches, saving time on research and writing. The company also publishes research about the relationship between journalists and PR.

item.title: MyHeritage
item.description:
MyHeritage is a genealogy service. Users create a tree, and the site suggests matches in historical records and in other members’ trees, helping them find ancestors and living relatives. A DNA test adds ethnicity estimates and connects users with genetic relatives.

The company is known for photo tools. It can colorize black-and-white pictures, enhance old photos, and animate faces in family photographs, which went viral and made genealogy more emotional for many users. Other AI features transcribe and search documents.

item.title: NationBuilder
item.description:
NationBuilder is designed for people building a movement. A campaign or organization keeps records of supporters, volunteers, and donors in one database, runs a website, sends email and texts, organizes events, and takes donations. Having everything together helps small teams manage a large network.

Tools support organizing, such as lists, tags, and tasks for volunteers, and reporting on progress toward goals. AI features help draft messages and summarize supporter information. The platform is used by campaigns, community groups, and associations around the world.

item.title: nCino
item.description:
nCino is cloud banking software. A bank uses it to manage the full lending process, from application to documents, analysis, approval, and closing, replacing paper and email chains. It covers commercial, consumer, and mortgage lending and account opening.

AI and automation reduce manual work. Models extract financial data from documents, assess credit risk, and flag items for review, and agents help with tasks like drafting credit memos. Dashboards give management visibility across the portfolio.

item.title: Notarize (Proof)
item.description:
Notarize brought notarization online. A signer uploads a document, verifies identity by scanning an ID and answering questions, joins a video call with a commissioned notary, and signs digitally. The notary applies a digital seal and the document is stored securely, making a process that required an in-person visit possible from home.

The company, now operating as Proof, expanded into broader identity and signature products for businesses, including title and escrow, banks, and real estate. AI-based checks examine ID documents and confirm that a live person is present, which helps resist fraud.

item.title: Noterro
item.description:
Noterro is built for small bodywork and rehab practices. Clients book online and fill in intake forms before arriving, and therapists record sessions with notes. An AI feature turns a few prompts into a structured SOAP note, saving time at the end of each appointment.

Other tools cover everyday needs: scheduling, reminders, payments, packages and memberships, and insurance claims where relevant. Reports track revenue and client retention.

Noterro is paid, with plans per practitioner. It is aimed at solo practitioners and small clinics. Alternatives include Jane, Cliniko, MassageBook, Vagaro, and SimplePractice. Noterro suits manual therapists who want simpler admin.

item.title: nTopology
item.description:
nTopology, now often shortened to nTop, is engineering design software. Traditional CAD builds shapes from sketches and features, while nTop uses fields and rules to generate complex internal structures, such as lattices whose density changes with stress. This produces lighter and stronger parts that suit 3D printing.

Workflows can be saved and reused, so a design process is captured as a repeatable recipe that updates when inputs change. It connects to simulation and manufacturing tools, and supports optimization where the software generates shapes that meet loads and constraints.

item.title: Nutrium
item.description:
Nutrium helps nutrition professionals run a practice. They manage clients, schedule appointments, and keep records of measurements and goals, while clients use an app to log meals and see their plan. A food database with nutrient data supports analysis and meal planning.

AI speeds up plan creation by proposing menus that fit a client’s calorie and nutrient targets and preferences, which the dietitian then adjusts. Reports and communication tools keep clients engaged between visits.

item.title: Paperpal
item.description:
Paperpal is designed for researchers. It works in a web editor, a Word add-in, and a browser extension, checking grammar, clarity, and tone against academic conventions. Suggestions are tuned to scholarly writing, where general tools may flag correct technical phrasing.

Beyond language editing, it offers help with paraphrasing, summarizing, and reference management, plus a literature search feature that finds papers and answers questions with citations. A journal submission check reviews manuscripts against common requirements before submission.

item.title: Perfect365
item.description:
Perfect365 started as a makeover app. A user takes or uploads a selfie, and face detection places virtual makeup, such as lipstick, eyeshadow, and foundation, or changes hair color. Retouching tools smooth skin and adjust features.

Salons and beauty professionals use virtual try-on to help clients picture a result, which supports decisions and sales. It is also popular for social media photos.

Heavy retouching can distort self-image, so use with care, and check the privacy policy since the app processes face photos. It is free with ads and paid options. Alternatives include YouCam Makeup, Facetune, FaceApp, and Modiface. Perfect365 suits casual users and beauty professionals.

item.title: Physna
item.description:
Physna is a geometric search engine. Instead of searching for a part by name, a user uploads a model and the system finds others with similar shapes, even if they were named differently or came from different CAD programs. This helps find existing parts to reuse and detect duplicates.

Manufacturers use it to cut costs from redundant parts, speed up quoting, and manage large catalogs. It also supports analysis such as comparing a design with a reference and checking for intellectual property overlap.

item.title: Productboard
item.description:
Productboard is a product management platform. Feedback from many sources flows into a central place, where it is linked to features and customers. Product managers see which problems come up most and who is asking, which grounds roadmap decisions in evidence.

AI helps process the volume of input. It groups similar requests, summarizes calls and tickets, and drafts specs and release notes. Prioritization frameworks score ideas against objectives, and roadmaps can be shared with stakeholders at different levels of detail.

item.title: project44
item.description:
project44 is a supply chain visibility platform. It gathers location and status data from trucks, rail, ocean, and air carriers, merges it into one view, and shows shippers where each shipment is. Predictive ETAs account for traffic, weather, and port conditions.

Alerts flag delays early, so teams can reroute or notify customers. The platform also offers tools for appointment scheduling, drayage, and analytics on carrier performance, and AI features automate routine tracking tasks and communication.

item.title: Propeller Aero
item.description:
Propeller serves construction, mining, and quarry sites. A drone flies a site, often with ground control targets, and the images are processed into accurate maps and 3D models. Users measure stockpiles, cut and fill volumes, and compare the site with design plans.

Dashboards share progress with project teams, and tools track haul roads, compare surveys over time, and generate reports for clients. Its PPK-enabled hardware and workflow aim to improve accuracy and reduce the need for ground control points.

item.title: Quizgecko
item.description:
Quizgecko speeds up quiz writing. A user pastes text, uploads a file, or links to a page, chooses a question type and difficulty, and the AI generates a set of questions with answers. Quizzes can be edited, shared with a link, embedded, or exported to learning platforms.

Teachers use it for classroom quizzes and practice tests, trainers for compliance checks, and students for self-testing. Flashcards and other study formats are available, and analytics show how learners performed.

item.title: Quorum
item.description:
Quorum is a public affairs platform. Users track legislation and regulations, follow lawmakers, and keep a record of their outreach, all in one system. Alerts notify them when a bill moves or a hearing is scheduled, and a database of officials supports advocacy campaigns.

AI summarizes long bills, flags relevant provisions, and helps draft messages and reports. Constituent engagement tools let organizations mobilize supporters to contact officials. Teams use the data to plan strategy and measure impact.

item.title: Qventus
item.description:
Qventus works on hospital operations. It connects to scheduling and records systems, forecasts demand in the emergency room, operating rooms, and inpatient units, and flags bottlenecks like discharges that are running late or beds that will not be ready. It recommends actions for staff.

Automation is part of the pitch. The platform can complete tasks like reaching out to patients for scheduling or following up on referrals, and AI agents handle routine work in areas such as surgical scheduling and call centers. The goal is to improve access while easing staff burden.

item.title: Rayyan
item.description:
Rayyan streamlines a laborious step in evidence synthesis. Researchers import search results from databases, and multiple reviewers screen titles and abstracts, marking papers as included or excluded, often blind to each other’s decisions. The tool tracks conflicts and helps resolve them.

Machine learning ranks the unscreened papers by likelihood of relevance, so the likely includes surface earlier and screening can end sooner. Highlighting of keywords and filtering by terms speeds reading. Newer features use AI to assist with extraction and summaries.

item.title: Reaxys
item.description:
Reaxys is a chemistry research database from Elsevier. A chemist can search by structure, reaction, or property and find experimental data on compounds, along with the reactions used to make them and the sources. This helps plan syntheses and avoid repeating known work.

Predictive synthesis tools propose routes to a target molecule by combining literature data with machine learning, ranking options by feasibility. It also covers properties, bioactivity, and patent chemistry, serving drug discovery and materials work.

item.title: Rogo
item.description:
Rogo focuses on the work of junior bankers and analysts, who spend hours digging through filings, transcripts, and data. A user asks a question in plain language, such as how a company’s margins compare with peers, and Rogo retrieves and analyzes the sources, citing where numbers came from.

It connects to financial data providers and a firm’s internal documents, produces outputs like comps and summaries, and fits into the workflow with tools such as Excel and PowerPoint. Security and compliance features suit regulated firms.

item.title: Sales Boomerang
item.description:
Sales Boomerang helps brokers stay in touch at the right time. It connects to a broker’s client list, watches for signals such as changes in credit, equity, or market rates, and alerts the broker when a former client might benefit from refinancing or a new purchase.

That turns a dormant database into leads. Automated outreach can follow, with messages personalized to the situation. Brokers use it to generate repeat and referral business without constant manual review.

item.title: Seequent
item.description:
Seequent software helps geologists understand what lies underground. Its flagship Leapfrog creates 3D models from drill holes, geophysics, and maps, so teams can see ore bodies and structures, plan drilling, and estimate resources. Other products handle geotechnical data, groundwater, and geophysical modeling.

Mining companies, geotechnical engineers, and environmental consultants use these models for decisions. Cloud tools allow collaboration and centralized data management, and newer features apply machine learning to modeling tasks.

item.title: Shift Technology
item.description:
Shift Technology serves insurers. When a claim arrives, its models assess the likelihood of fraud, explain the red flags, and route the case, so investigators spend time on the suspicious ones while clean claims are paid quickly.

The company extends the approach to underwriting, subrogation, and customer service, and has added generative AI agents that help adjusters summarize files and handle routine tasks. Its customers include large carriers around the world.

item.title: SimplePractice
item.description:
SimplePractice is widely used by solo and small group private practices. Clients book appointments online, complete intake forms in a portal, and join video sessions, while clinicians keep notes, treatment plans, and billing in the same system. Insurance claims can be submitted electronically.

AI features help clinicians write progress notes from session details and speed up documentation, which is a chief burden for therapists. The platform offers reminders, reporting, and a client app for messaging and payments.

item.title: Smartify
item.description:
Smartify is an app for cultural venues. A visitor opens it in a partner museum, scans an artwork with the camera, and the app identifies it and shows background, artist information, and audio commentary. Collections can be saved for later.

Museums use it to enrich visits without installing hardware, and to learn what visitors engage with. The platform includes tools for creating tours and for accessibility. Some partners are major institutions.

item.title: Spectora
item.description:
Spectora is software for home inspection businesses. Inspectors document a property on a phone or tablet, adding photos, notes, and ratings, and Spectora compiles a professional report that can be delivered to clients and agents. Scheduling, agreements, and payment tools run the business side.

AI speeds up the slow part. It helps summarize defects, produce clear language for findings, and organize repair requests, and voice dictation turns spoken notes into text. Reports include summaries that buyers and agents can use during negotiations.

item.title: Stitch Fix
item.description:
Stitch Fix popularized personal styling by mail. A new client fills out a style profile, and a stylist assisted by algorithms selects pieces from many brands, ships them in a box, and the client keeps what they like and returns the rest. Feedback on each item improves later selections, and clients can also shop items directly through a browsing experience.

Data science has been central to the company’s identity. Algorithms analyze client preferences, item attributes, and inventory to predict what each customer will like, and stylists apply judgment and personal touches. Generative AI tools help create outfit suggestions and visual try-on features, and the company has also experimented with ways to let customers shop without a stylist.

item.title: StyleSeat
item.description:
StyleSeat serves independent beauty professionals. Clients search for stylists, browse portfolios and reviews, and book appointments, while professionals manage their calendar, take deposits, and process payments through the platform.

The marketplace helps new clients find providers, and the business tools handle reminders, no-show protection, and client records. Recommendations use location and preference data to match clients.

StyleSeat has a subscription for professionals and fees on some transactions. Fees for marketplace clients can be a concern for stylists with an existing following. Alternatives include Vagaro, Fresha, Booksy, Square Appointments, and Glossgenius. StyleSeat suits independent stylists and barbers.

item.title: Tracers
item.description:
Tracers is an investigative data service. A user enters a name, address, or other identifier, and the platform returns linked records about people and businesses, such as addresses, relatives, liens, and court filings. Matching algorithms connect pieces of information.

Customers include private investigators, attorneys, collections agencies, and law enforcement. Access is restricted by law in many cases and requires a permissible purpose, and results have limits in accuracy.

Tracers is sold on subscription and per search. Using such data raises privacy and legal issues, and background checks used for employment or housing are subject to consumer reporting laws. Alternatives include LexisNexis Accurint, TLOxp, Thomson Reuters CLEAR, and IRB Search. Tracers suits licensed investigative professionals.

item.title: Tractable
item.description:
Tractable applies computer vision to insurance claims. After an accident, a policyholder or repairer uploads photos, and the AI identifies damaged parts and estimates repair costs, speeding up decisions that used to wait for an inspection.

Insurers use it to settle simple claims fast, to triage complex ones, and to detect inconsistencies. The company has expanded to property damage after disasters and to the used-parts and repair industries.

Tractable is sold to insurers and repair networks on enterprise contracts. Automated estimates affect people’s payments, so fairness, accuracy, and appeal routes matter. Alternatives include CCC Intelligent Solutions, Solera, Mitchell, Shift Technology, and Cambridge Mobile Telematics. Tractable suits insurers speeding up claims.

item.title: Transkribus
item.description:
Transkribus is built for historical documents. Archivists and researchers upload scans of handwritten or old printed material, and the platform transcribes them with models that can be trained on a specific hand or period. The result is searchable text that can be corrected and exported.

It grew from European research projects and is now run by a cooperative, READ-COOP. Thousands of archives, libraries, and genealogists use it, and public models cover many languages and eras. AI search finds words across collections.

item.title: Trinka
item.description:
Trinka is built for scholarly and professional documents. It reviews text for grammar, style, and consistency with academic conventions, and understands field-specific terms in areas like medicine, engineering, and law. Suggestions explain why a change is recommended.

Extra tools check for plagiarism and consistency, offer paraphrasing, and run publication readiness checks. Plugins work with Microsoft Word and browsers, and a web editor is available.

Trinka has a free tier and paid plans. Authors should follow journal policies on AI-assisted editing. Alternatives include Paperpal, Grammarly, Writefull, Wordvice AI, and QuillBot. Trinka suits researchers and students polishing manuscripts.

item.title: Upheal
item.description:
Upheal helps therapists reduce paperwork. With client consent, the tool records or transcribes a session and drafts a note in the clinician’s preferred format, which they review and sign. It can summarize progress over time and suggest treatment plan updates.

The product emphasizes privacy and compliance with health data rules, and offers a free tier for solo practitioners. Session insights, such as talk time and themes, give feedback to the clinician.

item.title: Vagaro
item.description:
Vagaro runs the front desk for beauty and wellness businesses. Clients book online or through a marketplace app, staff manage calendars, take payments, and track inventory. Reminders and no-show protection reduce lost appointments.

Marketing tools include email and text campaigns, loyalty programs, and a presence on the Vagaro marketplace. AI answers calls and messages, helps book appointments, and suggests promotions.

Vagaro charges a monthly fee per business, with add-ons and payment processing fees. Alternatives include Fresha, Booksy, StyleSeat, Square Appointments, and Mindbody. Vagaro suits salons, spas, and studios.

item.title: VidIQ
item.description:
vidIQ helps YouTubers grow. A browser extension adds data to YouTube pages and Studio, showing keyword scores, competitor stats, and tags used by successful videos. Research tools find topics with demand and low competition.

AI features suggest video ideas, titles, and thumbnails, write descriptions, and give feedback on videos. Analytics track subscriber growth and performance, and a coach feature gives guidance.

vidIQ has a free plan and paid tiers. Optimization scores are guides, and content quality drives results. Alternatives include TubeBuddy, Morningfame, Social Blade, and YouTube’s own research tools. vidIQ suits creators optimizing a channel.

item.title: Visier
item.description:
Visier gathers data from HR systems into a model built for workforce questions. HR teams and managers explore metrics such as turnover, hiring speed, diversity, and compensation, and see how they vary by team and over time. Prebuilt analyses save the effort of building reports from scratch.

AI predicts who may leave, models the effect of decisions, and answers questions in plain language through a virtual assistant. Planning tools support headcount and cost scenarios, and integrations pull data from systems such as Workday and SAP.

item.title: Vivino
item.description:
Vivino started as a wine label scanner. A user photographs a bottle, and the app recognizes it, showing the average rating, tasting notes, price ranges, and what other drinkers say. This helps shoppers choose in stores and restaurants.

The app has become a marketplace as well, where users can buy wines from partner merchants. A taste profile learns from your ratings and recommends bottles, and features include food pairing suggestions and a cellar to track wines.

item.title: Wildbook
item.description:
Wildbook turns photos into population data. Scientists and citizen scientists upload pictures of animals such as whale sharks, giraffes, and sea turtles, and the software recognizes individuals by distinctive markings, such as spot patterns or fin shapes, and links sightings over time.

That reveals movement, survival, and population size without physically tagging animals. The platform supports many species, with separate databases for each, and photos from tourists and social media can contribute.

item.title: Yoodli
item.description:
Yoodli is an AI speech coach. A user records themselves or practices with an AI role-play partner, and the tool analyzes delivery: filler words, speaking rate, pauses, and word choice, and gives a report with suggestions and trends over time.

Role-play scenarios cover interviews, sales calls, and presentations, where an AI plays the other party and responds. Organizations use Yoodli for sales and leadership training, with private practice that removes the embarrassment of rehearsing in front of others.

item.title: Zycus
item.description:
Zycus is a source-to-pay suite. Companies manage supplier onboarding, sourcing events, contracts, purchase orders, and invoice processing in one platform, giving procurement teams visibility and control over spend.

AI agents assist with the work. They read contracts to extract terms, detect anomalies in pricing or invoices, suggest suppliers, and draft communications. Analytics show savings and compliance.

Zycus is sold to large enterprises on subscription. Alternatives include Coupa, SAP Ariba, Jaggaer, Ivalua, and GEP. Zycus suits procurement teams at large organizations.

item.title: OpenAI Dots
item.description: Dots move ChatGPT from a tool you open to an assistant that keeps working. Each dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can carry out tasks on websites and in apps without tying up your device. You give it goals, such as keeping track of your inbox, preparing for meetings, or monitoring a project, and it works in the background, checking back when it needs input. Over time it learns from your feedback.

item.title: Cuey
item.description:
Cuey is a tool for comparing chatbots. From a sidebar in Chrome, you type a prompt once and it goes to services such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini that you are logged into, with the responses displayed together. A view highlights where the answers agree and differ, which is useful for fact-checking and choosing the best phrasing.

It includes a library of saved prompts and a memory feature so context can follow you from one model to another. Because it works with the chat interfaces you already use, it does not need separate API keys. The developer, Llama Valley Inc, states that prompts and responses are not stored on its servers.

item.title: Momentic Mo
item.description:
Mo takes an exploratory approach to testing. Instead of writing scripts for each test, a team points Mo at an app and supplies login credentials, and AI agents navigate the interface, trying flows, entering unusual inputs, and checking for errors or broken behavior. The agents report what they find.

Momentic’s wider platform helps teams write and maintain end-to-end tests in natural language, which reduces upkeep when interfaces change. Mo complements that by finding issues no one thought to test, like a human tester poking around.

item.title: NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform
item.description:
The platform responds to a security worry: autonomous agents that can run commands and access data need limits that a compromised agent cannot disable. OpenShell is an open-source runtime that places each agent in its own sandbox with policy-based permissions, and a prover checks that granted permissions cannot combine into something the operator did not intend.

Sentry adds enforcement outside the agent’s machine. It runs on BlueField data processing units, which sit apart from the host, so it can watch behavior and isolate an agent quickly even if the host is compromised. NVIDIA has described it as a reference design, with many partners integrating the pieces.

item.title: QA Wolf
item.description:
QA Wolf offers testing as a service. Instead of a company writing and maintaining its own automated tests, QA Wolf’s team creates Playwright tests for the critical flows, runs them in parallel on every release, and fixes tests when the app changes. They report real bugs, and filter flaky failures.

AI generates and repairs tests, while engineers verify results. The aim is high coverage without the burden of test maintenance, which often overwhelms small teams. Tests are written in open frameworks, so customers own the code.

item.title: TypingMind
item.description:
TypingMind is a front end for AI models. A user supplies API keys, and gets a clean chat app with conversation folders, prompt libraries, and tools. Pay-per-use API pricing can be cheaper than several subscriptions, especially for light users.

Features include support for multiple models in one place, custom assistants, plugins, and knowledge uploads, and teams can share setups with controlled access. It is a paid product with a one-time or subscription license depending on the plan.

item.title: ByteAsk
item.description:
ByteAsk positions itself around a less glamorous part of software work. Most AI coding tools focus on writing new code, but a large share of an engineer’s time goes into finding why something breaks, why a service is slow, and keeping older systems healthy. A tool focused on that work would read logs, traces, and code to find causes and suggest fixes.

That area is promising because debugging depends on context that general assistants lack, such as how a particular system behaves in production. It also carries risk, since a wrong fix can make things worse, so suggested changes need review and testing before they ship.

item.title: Ando
item.description:
Ando rethinks team chat for a workplace where software agents work next to people. In most chat tools, AI is an add-on bot. In Ando, agents have identities, inboxes, and permissions, and they can join channels, read ongoing conversations, and message teammates, just like human members.

The product has the familiar parts of a messaging platform, including channels, direct messages, group conversations, and calls. The difference is how agents are treated: a person can assign work to an agent in a thread, and the agent can respond, ask questions, and report back. Teams can bring agents built on different models.

item.title: Scholé
item.description:
Scholé rethinks workplace learning. Instead of asking employees to finish courses on the side, it delivers short, relevant learning moments tied to real tasks, adapting to what a person already knows and needs to do. Principles from learning science, such as practice and spaced repetition, shape the design.

Teams can use it to build skills in areas like communication, sales, or technical topics, with AI creating content and feedback. The idea is learning that fits into work and sticks.

item.title: Lettu
item.description:
Lettu is a platform for brands, agencies, and creators who work together. Influencer and creator campaigns involve briefs, contracts, approvals, payments, and usage rights, which are often handled in scattered emails. Lettu puts these into one workflow with legal templates drafted by lawyers.

The platform helps brands and agencies draft briefs, agree terms, track deliverables, and manage rights, such as how long content can be used. It draws on the law firm’s experience in advertising and media law, and AI features speed up drafting and review.

item.title: Astra for Law
item.description:
Astra for Law packages OpenAI’s model for legal work. Rather than a separate model, it pairs a general model with a dedicated search index of U.S. case law, statutes, regulations, and court rules, and instructions shaped for legal analysis and drafting. The goal is research answers that are grounded in sources a lawyer can check.

Access has been limited. OpenAI offered it first to selected firms through a trusted access program, with plans to make it available to legal technology companies through the API so they can build it into their own products. Partner plugins connect it to tools used in legal practice, such as document review, practice management, and document management systems.

item.title: Claude Docs
item.description:
Claude Docs brings document writing into the chat. Instead of copying an answer from a conversation into another app, you ask Claude to draft a report, memo, or plan, and it appears as a document you can edit beside the conversation. You can revise it by typing changes directly or by asking Claude to rework sections.

Documents are stored in the Artifacts tab, so they are easy to find later and update across sessions. When the draft is ready, it can be exported to common formats such as Word, PDF, Google Docs, or Markdown. The tool handles headings, lists, and tables, and it works with files and context shared in the conversation.

item.title: Claude Slides
item.description:
Claude Slides makes decks from a conversation. You describe the audience and the point of the presentation, share notes or source files, and Claude produces a set of slides with an outline, text, and layout. You can then ask for changes, such as a different order, a tighter message, or new visuals, and edit individual slides directly.

The finished deck can be presented from within Claude or exported to PowerPoint or PDF for use elsewhere. Because it lives in the same place as the conversation, you can pull information from uploaded documents and revise based on feedback without switching tools. It sits alongside Claude’s other creation features, including Docs.

item.title: Enlive
item.description:
Enlive is a prompt layer. Instead of writing a long, careful prompt, a user types a brief request, and Enlive expands it with relevant context, structure, and instructions before sending it to a model. The idea is to get better answers from people who are not prompt engineers.

It works across multiple models and tracks preferences, such as tone and format, so later requests fit the user’s habits. This addresses the common experience that vague prompts return vague answers. For power users it can save the time spent rewriting prompts.

item.title: Grok Bot
item.description:
Grok Bot takes a different shape from a chat window. A user creates named bots and assigns them tasks, and each bot runs in the cloud, keeps working after the user closes their laptop, and can sign into apps and use a browser to complete work. Examples include handling inbox tasks, researching topics, and running routine workflows.

The product emphasizes persistence. Bots remember context over time and report back, and the cloud computer gives them a place to store files and run tools. It is positioned for both individuals and businesses, with a business version aimed at agents that log into company applications.

item.title: MagicShot
item.description:
MagicShot takes an all-in-one approach to generative media. Rather than paying for a different service for each task, users get a single workspace for generating images, creating video, building avatars, making product shots, and producing voiceovers, all drawing on one pool of credits.

That suits marketers and small businesses who need a bit of everything. Tools include background replacement, upscaling, style transfer, and templates for ads and social posts. Convenience comes with some compromise, as individual tools may be less advanced than specialized products.

item.title: MosMos
item.description:
MosMos is a dictation and meeting tool for Mac. A user speaks and text appears in the active app, formatted to fit the context: casual in a chat, structured in a document, code-friendly in an editor. A personal glossary learns names and technical terms, reducing repeated mistakes.

In meetings, MosMos can record and transcribe with labels for each speaker and produce notes and action items afterward. Combining dictation and meeting features in one app saves switching between tools.

item.title: Sider Omni Sidebar
item.description:
Sider began as a browser sidebar for chatting with AI about web pages. Omni Sidebar extends the idea to the whole Mac: a panel that sees the content in the active app and lets users ask questions, summarize, draft replies, or take actions without copying and pasting.

The assistant supports several underlying models and can work with files and screenshots. For people who live in email, documents, and spreadsheets, an assistant that sees the same screen saves steps.

item.title: Google CC
item.description:
CC acts like a morning assistant. Each day it sends an email, called Your Day Ahead, that pulls together calendar events, important messages, bills, and documents relevant to the day. You reply to the email to ask for changes, such as adding an event or digging into a topic, and CC acts on it.

It connects to a user’s Gmail, Calendar, and Drive and can also use the web for context. Because it works through email, there is no new app to learn. Google has expanded the experiment to support shared use by members of a household, with each person connecting their own accounts.

item.title: Meta Muse
item.description: Muse is Meta’s step from a chat assistant to an agent that acts on your behalf. You ask it to do something, such as arrange a trip, draft and send an email, or handle a multi-step errand, and it works across apps and websites to complete the job. Each user’s agent runs in a secure virtual machine, so it can continue working after you leave the app and come back when it needs a decision.

item.title: Free AI Face Swap
item.description:
Free AI Face Swap lets a user upload two photos and exchange the faces. The tool detects faces, aligns them, and blends the result. It runs in the browser, supports common image formats, and offers extra effects around face editing.

People use face swaps for entertainment, memes, and creative projects. The same technology can be misused to create misleading or non-consensual images, so use only photos of people who have agreed, and never use swaps to deceive or harass. Many places have laws about deepfakes and intimate image abuse.

item.title: MagiCrew
item.description:
MagiCrew packages agent capabilities in one open-source system. A general agent can plan and complete tasks with tools, a visual workflow editor lets users build repeatable processes, and messaging and collaboration features let teams work with agents in shared spaces.

Because it is open source, organizations can host it themselves and adapt it, which appeals to teams with privacy requirements or specific needs. It extends an existing open-source project, which gives it a base of users and code to build on.

item.title: Almanac
item.description:
Almanac builds memory for an AI agent. Once you connect work accounts, it reads messages, calendar events, documents, and code activity and compiles what it learns into a wiki covering people, projects, and decisions. The wiki updates as new information arrives, so the agent does not start from zero each time.

The agent then uses that knowledge to do work. Teammates can send requests through tools such as Slack, and it checks the wiki for context before acting, which aims to reduce the repeated explaining that other assistants need. Connections can be personal or shared, so a company can decide how much of its information the agent sees.

item.title: Aloud
item.description:
Aloud addresses the gap between what a developer means and what ends up in a written bug report or feature request. It records voice, screen, and a live transcript while someone talks through an app the way they naturally would, pointing at elements and changing their mind mid-sentence. It then converts the recording into a clean set of instructions.

The output is formatted so coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex can act on it directly. The tool flags anything that could be read two ways and attaches relevant screenshots, which cuts down on back-and-forth. Speech transcription runs locally through Whisper, so recordings stay on the Mac and are not uploaded, which matters for work on client or proprietary code.

item.title: ChatGPT Atlas
item.description:
Atlas puts ChatGPT inside the browser. A sidebar assistant can see the page you are on, so you can ask it to summarize an article, explain a table, compare products across tabs, or draft a reply in context. The address bar can also act as a chat prompt, and the browser can remember context from your browsing if you turn that on.

Agent mode goes further. The assistant can take actions on your behalf, such as navigating to a site, filling in a form, or doing research across several pages, while you watch and can take over. This capability is powerful and also risky, since web pages can contain instructions meant to trick an agent, a problem known as prompt injection.

item.title: Codex
item.description:
Codex works as a software engineering agent. A developer describes a task, such as fixing a bug or adding a feature, and Codex explores the code, makes a plan, edits files, and runs tests or linters to verify the result. It reports back with a summary of what it changed and why.

It comes in several forms. A command line tool runs on the developer’s machine, a desktop app manages multiple tasks, extensions integrate with editors like VS Code, and a cloud version in ChatGPT runs tasks in isolated sandboxes, often in parallel, and can propose pull requests on GitHub. Configuration files let teams give the agent project instructions.

item.title: GitNexus
item.description:
GitNexus gives coding agents a map of a codebase. It analyzes repositories and builds a graph in which nodes are symbols, files, functions, and services, and edges show how they relate, such as which function calls another. Agents query the graph over the Model Context Protocol to answer questions like what will break if this function changes.

The aim is more reliable context than searching text or embeddings, which can miss relationships. The graph can span multiple repositories, which helps in organizations with many services. It works with different agents and editors, and the vendor claims it lowers cost and errors.

item.title: Magic Hour
item.description:
Magic Hour brings several AI video tools together. A user can animate a still image, generate a clip from a prompt, convert a video into an anime or painted style, sync a character’s lips to audio, or swap faces. The tools run in the browser and export short videos for social media.

It is aimed at creators and marketers who want a variety of effects without learning several apps. A credit system covers the different features, and templates help with common formats such as memes and talking-head videos.

item.title: OpenCode
item.description:
OpenCode is a coding agent that works in a developer’s terminal. It reads a repository, plans changes, edits files, and runs commands, with a text interface for conversation. The same engine also runs behind a desktop app, editor extension, and web client.

Provider freedom is the main appeal. Users connect models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others, or open models run locally, and can switch between them. Configuration files add project rules, custom agents, and Model Context Protocol tools, and sessions can be shared.

item.title: QueryStory
item.description:
QueryStory approaches analytics with agents. A team connects its data sources and describes the business, such as its metrics and definitions, and then asks questions in natural language. The agents write queries, analyze results, and respond with explanations and visuals.

The point is to go beyond a static chart. When a number moves, a user can ask why, and the agent investigates by looking at breakdowns and related data. Business context helps the agent interpret questions the way an analyst on the team would.

item.title: Viktor
item.description:
Viktor lives where teams already talk. Instead of a separate app, a colleague mentions Viktor in a channel and asks for something, such as pulling numbers from a dashboard, building a report, or writing a script, and it replies in the thread. It watches how the team works and picks up context over time.

It connects to a very large number of business tools, so it can read from and act in systems like CRMs, analytics, and ad platforms, and it can produce artifacts such as documents and simple web apps. Skills can be added for specialized work.

item.title: Zetik
item.description:
Zetik is a personal research assistant. A user picks topics, and the system monitors many source types, ranks what matters, and delivers a concise brief, so they stay informed without scanning feeds. It aims to surface signal across places that are hard to follow manually.

This suits founders, investors, and researchers who track fast-moving fields. Summaries need to link back to sources, and personalization improves as the tool learns what the user finds relevant.

item.title: Careforce AI
item.description:
Careforce provides AI workers for healthcare administration. Agents place outbound calls and texts to patients, such as to schedule overdue screenings, confirm appointments, and collect information before a visit. They handle follow-up and rescheduling, which often falls through in busy offices.

The company says its agents support many languages and can work across scheduling systems and payer portals, which lets clinics reach patients who might otherwise be missed. Scripts are configurable for different campaigns, such as preventive care outreach and post-operative check-ins.

item.title: DeepSeek Harness
item.description:
DeepSeek Harness is a framework for running agents that work on code. It provides the loop that lets a model plan, call tools, read and edit files, run shell commands, and report back, similar in purpose to terminal agents from other labs. Its notable design choice is that nearly every part is a plugin: the model adapter, tool registry, session log, and the agent loop itself can be replaced.

It includes presets for common setups, such as a standard coding agent with filesystem and shell tools, web search, subagents, and a planning mode, and a mode for building custom presets. Sandboxing uses the operating system’s own mechanisms to limit what the agent can touch. Although DeepSeek made it, it can connect to models from other providers.

item.title: Encore AI
item.description:
Encore AI builds on conversation data. It analyzes recordings of calls and chats to learn which behaviors lead to good outcomes, such as how top reps handle objections or open a conversation. Those patterns become the basis for AI agents that talk with customers.

The agents can take calls or messages themselves or support human reps with live guidance. The idea is to scale the best performers’ approach across a team instead of relying on training alone. Companies with large volumes of calls and recorded history are the target.

item.title: Ivo
item.description:
Ivo is an AI contract review tool built for in-house legal teams. A lawyer opens an incoming contract, and Ivo compares it with the team’s preferred positions, flags issues, and suggests redlines in the document, using the editor the lawyer already works in.

Beyond review, Ivo has added tools to manage the whole flow. Business users submit requests, contracts are routed to the right reviewers, negotiations are tracked, and approvals are collected. A repository holds executed agreements for analysis.

item.title: Meta Muse Code
item.description:
Muse Code is Meta’s entry into agentic coding. A developer starts it in a project folder, describes a task, and the agent explores the code, plans changes, edits files, and runs tests, working across a repository rather than on single files. It is powered by a Meta model tuned for coding.

Meta presents it as a lower-cost option next to tools from Anthropic and OpenAI, and it runs from the command line on macOS and Linux. Features such as running sub-agents in parallel aim at larger tasks. The tool was released in beta, so expect changes.

item.title: Natural
item.description:
Natural addresses a gap in agent infrastructure: how an AI agent pays for things. Through its API, developers create an account for an agent, fund it, set spending rules, and let it pay vendors, receive money, or issue virtual cards for purchases.

Controls matter, since a spending agent can cause damage. Limits, approvals, and logs let the owner decide what an agent may buy and see what it did. The company positions this as payments infrastructure for a future where agents transact with each other and with businesses.

item.title: OpenAI Daybreak
item.description:
Daybreak gives defenders access to frontier AI for security work. Approved organizations use models for tasks such as triaging incidents, analyzing malware, validating patches, and hunting for vulnerabilities, with workflows designed for security teams.

OpenAI split access into tiers. A defender tier provides frontier models without some of the safeguards that might block legitimate security prompts, and a more specialized tier provides models trained for higher-risk testing such as vulnerability research and exploit validation. Access is limited to vetted individuals and organizations.

item.title: Cloudflare Kitesurf
item.description:
Kitesurf rethinks the browser for software. Most automation tools control a full desktop browser, which is heavy and built around human use. Kitesurf is a lean browser written to run inside Cloudflare’s Workers platform, so an agent can open pages, read them, and click or type without the overhead of a complete Chrome instance.

It works with existing tools. Clients that use Puppeteer, Playwright, or the Model Context Protocol can connect to it through Cloudflare’s browser service with small changes. The design treats every page as untrusted and starts each session fresh, which suits agent security. Cloudflare says it uses less memory than Chromium in its tests.

item.title: BrowserStack Test Companion
item.description:
Test Companion is an AI agent for quality assurance. Instead of a separate dashboard, it works in the developer’s editor, where it can generate test scripts from a description or from the code, run them on BrowserStack’s device and browser cloud, and investigate failures.

Maintenance is a major use. Tests break when interfaces change, and fixing them takes time. The agent can update selectors, adjust steps, and rerun, which reduces the upkeep that makes automated testing costly. It works with common frameworks and connects to BrowserStack’s testing infrastructure.

item.title: Comet
item.description:
Comet makes the assistant part of the browser. Instead of copying content into a chatbot, users can ask questions about the page they are on, compare information across tabs, summarize a thread, or have the assistant search and collect results. Perplexity’s answer engine is the default way to search.

An agent mode lets the assistant take actions, such as filling in forms, managing a calendar or inbox, or completing a purchase flow, while the user watches and can step in. This gives it the power and the risks of any browsing agent, including exposure to prompt injection from malicious web pages.

item.title: Genspark
item.description:
Genspark started as an AI search engine and expanded into an agent workspace. A user states a goal, such as researching a market and building a presentation, and the Super Agent plans the steps, searches the web, uses tools, and produces outputs like slide decks, documents, spreadsheets, and media.

It combines several models and tools behind the scenes, and offers specialized agents for tasks like calling businesses on a user’s behalf, creating images and video, and building simple websites. Results appear in a workspace where users can review and edit them.

item.title: Google Antigravity
item.description:
Antigravity is Google’s take on an AI-first coding environment. Instead of a chat panel beside the editor, agents have direct access to the editor, the terminal, and a browser, so they can write code, run it, test the result in a browser, and report back with artifacts such as plans, screenshots, and recordings that show what they did.

Developers can run several agents in parallel and manage them from a control view. Later versions added background tasks that run on a schedule and a standalone command line tool. The environment uses Google’s Gemini models and can work with other models.

item.title: Kiro
item.description:
Kiro is built around spec-driven development. A developer describes a feature, and Kiro produces a requirements document, a technical design, and a task list. The developer reviews and edits these, and the agent then works through the tasks, writing code and tests. The idea is to keep an agent aligned with intent on larger work instead of improvising from chat.

The editor is based on Code OSS, so VS Code extensions and settings carry over. Hooks trigger agent actions on events such as saving a file, steering files give persistent guidance about a project, and support for the Model Context Protocol connects external tools. It uses Claude models through AWS.

item.title: OpenAI Presence
item.description:
Presence aims to let companies put OpenAI-powered agents on the front line of conversations. Businesses configure agents that talk with customers by phone or chat and handle employee requests, connecting them to company systems so they can look up information and take actions.

The platform combines the models with enterprise features: tools for building and testing agents, integrations, monitoring, and controls to keep agents within policy. It competes with specialized customer service AI vendors and with platforms from other model providers.

item.title: Algolia AI Search
item.description:
Algolia is a hosted search service known for speed. Developers send it their data, such as products, articles, or help center pages, and use its APIs and UI libraries to add search that responds as the user types, with typo tolerance, filters, and facets. Many e-commerce and media sites use it.

Its AI search layer extends that with newer methods. Hybrid search blends keyword matching with vector similarity so queries find results by meaning, and tools can personalize ranking from user behavior. Merchandisers can adjust relevance with business rules without code, and the platform supports retrieval for conversational and agent experiences, where an AI model answers using the retrieved content.

item.title: AMD ROCm
item.description:
ROCm is AMD’s answer to NVIDIA’s CUDA. It is a collection of software that lets programs use AMD graphics processors for general computing, including drivers, a compiler toolchain, math and communication libraries, and tools for debugging and profiling. Much of it is open source.

For AI work, the key piece is framework support. PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and others run on ROCm, and inference tools like vLLM and many model libraries have AMD builds. Developers can port CUDA code using HIP, a programming layer that resembles CUDA, and large cloud and supercomputer deployments use AMD Instinct accelerators with ROCm.

item.title: Baidu Qianfan
item.description:
Qianfan is Baidu’s cloud platform for building with large models. Companies can call Baidu’s ERNIE models and a selection of third-party and open models through a common API, then build applications such as chatbots, search over internal documents, and automated workflows. The platform covers the steps in between, including prompt engineering, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment.

It includes tools for agents and retrieval, with knowledge-base features that let applications answer from a company’s own data, plus plugins and workflows for connecting to business systems. Qianfan is used heavily within China, where Baidu offers local hosting and compliance with domestic regulations.

item.title: Braintrust
item.description:
Braintrust helps teams treat AI quality like software quality. Developers log each model call and agent step, then build datasets of test cases from real traffic. Scorers, including programmatic checks and language model judges, rate outputs, so a change to a prompt or model can be tested before it ships.

The product combines several pieces. A playground lets teams compare prompts and models side by side, experiments track results over time, and online monitoring scores production traffic and raises alerts. A gateway can route calls to different model providers, and collaboration features let engineers and non-engineers review outputs.

item.title: Cloudflare AI Gateway
item.description:
AI Gateway is a proxy for calls to language models. A developer points their app’s requests at a Cloudflare URL instead of the provider’s, and the gateway forwards them while recording what happens. This gives a dashboard of requests, tokens, costs, and errors across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

It adds control features. Caching returns stored answers for repeated requests to save money and time, rate limits protect budgets, and retries and fallbacks switch to another model when one fails. Logging helps debug prompts, and guardrails and key management features support security.

item.title: Cohere North
item.description:
North is Cohere’s platform for putting agents to work inside companies. Employees use a chat interface and can build agents without code for tasks in HR, finance, IT, and other areas, connecting them to the apps and documents they already use. Search across company data is powered by Cohere’s own retrieval technology.

Security and control are the main pitch. Organizations can deploy North in a private cloud, on premises, or in air-gapped settings, which appeals to banks, governments, and defense contractors with strict data rules. Cohere designs the models for enterprise use and works with customers on custom solutions.

item.title: Dataiku
item.description:
Dataiku aims to let analysts, data scientists, and engineers work in the same environment. Teams connect to data sources, clean and prepare data with visual recipes or code, build models, and deploy them as applications or services. The visual interface lowers the barrier for business users, while coders can use notebooks and libraries.

The platform has added tools for generative AI, including connecting to language models, building retrieval applications, and creating agents. Governance features track models and projects, assess risk, and document decisions, which large organizations need to meet internal and regulatory requirements.

item.title: DeepSeek
item.description: DeepSeek is an AI research company based in China whose models are released with their weights open, so anyone can download, run, and fine-tune them. Its general-purpose models handle chat, writing, and coding, and its reasoning models work through a problem step by step before answering. What got the industry’s attention was efficiency: DeepSeek’s models perform near the best closed systems on many math and coding benchmarks while being far cheaper to train and serve. Its technical papers, which describe how it did this, are widely read by other labs.

item.title: DeepSeek Chat
item.description:
DeepSeek Chat offers consumer access to DeepSeek’s language models. Users ask questions, draft text, write code, and work through math and logic, and a mode shows the model’s step-by-step reasoning before it gives an answer. It supports uploading files and searching the web.

DeepSeek drew wide attention when its models matched strong Western systems at much lower reported training cost, and it released the model weights openly, which let others run and study them. The chat app was one of the most downloaded in many countries soon after it launched.

item.title: Elastic AI Assistant
item.description:
Elastic AI Assistant is built into the Elastic stack, which many companies use for search, logs, and security monitoring. Users ask questions in plain language, such as what caused a spike in errors or what an alert means, and the assistant queries the data, explains findings, and suggests next steps.

For security teams, it helps triage alerts, write queries, and summarize incidents using the organization’s own data. For observability, it assists with investigating logs and metrics. Retrieval from indexed content grounds answers in real information, and administrators choose which language model provider to connect.

item.title: Figma Make
item.description:
Figma Make lets designers and product teams bring ideas to working form. A user describes an app, or starts from a Figma design, and the AI builds an interactive version using code. They can then edit it by chatting, adjusting on the canvas, or changing the code directly.

Because it connects to Figma, designs, components, and styles can serve as the starting point, which keeps results consistent with a design system. Teams use it to test ideas with realistic prototypes before involving engineering, and to share working demos with stakeholders. Backend features such as data storage let prototypes behave more like real apps.

item.title: FLUX
item.description: FLUX comes from Black Forest Labs, a company founded by researchers who previously worked on Stable Diffusion. Its models became popular because they produce sharp, detailed images that follow prompts closely, including difficult cases like readable text in a picture and complex scenes with several subjects. For many people, FLUX became the best open alternative to closed services such as Midjourney, because the weights for several versions can be downloaded and used locally.

item.title: Gemini Pro
item.description: Gemini Pro refers to the mid-sized models in Google’s Gemini family, positioned between the smaller, cheaper Flash models and the heaviest reasoning options. Google’s naming moves with each generation, but the idea stays the same: Pro is the version intended for demanding everyday work without the cost or delay of the very largest model. Gemini was designed from the start to take in several types of input at once, so the same model reads text, looks at images, listens to audio, and watches video rather than handing those jobs to separate systems.

item.title: GPT Image
item.description:
GPT Image brings image generation into the same model family that handles text. A user describes an image or uploads one to edit, and the model generates or modifies it, following detailed instructions and rendering readable text, which earlier image models struggled with. It can edit photos, change styles, and keep a subject consistent across images.

The model is available inside ChatGPT, where conversation lets users refine results step by step, and through the API for developers building apps. It replaced the DALL-E models in OpenAI’s lineup. Smaller and faster variants exist for cost-sensitive use.

item.title: Mistral
item.description: Mistral is Europe’s best-known frontier AI lab. It first drew attention by releasing compact open-weight models that matched or beat larger ones, and it has continued to release models in several sizes for chat, coding, reasoning, and vision. Some are free to download under permissive licenses, while its strongest models are offered through its API and Le Chat. Developers like that it gives them the choice to run models on their own hardware.

item.title: NVIDIA NIM
item.description:
