It provides a clean editor where you can draft with AI help, continue a passage, rewrite sections, and adjust tone or length, with a focus on staying in the flow of writing instead of juggling templates. The tool is aimed at bloggers, students, and fiction writers who want a collaborator that suggests next paragraphs or alternative phrasing.

It offers features common to AI writing tools, such as outline generation, summarizing, expanding ideas, and fixing grammar, with options to guide the style. Users can save projects and export their writing. The simple interface keeps focus on the text instead of a long menu of tools.

item.title: Chorus.ai
item.description:
Chorus records sales calls and video meetings and turns them into searchable transcripts. Managers can look through conversations to see what customers say about price, competitors, or objections, instead of relying on reps’ summaries. The tool tags topics, tracks talk time and question patterns, and highlights key moments, which makes it faster to review a call than to listen to the whole recording.

The AI layer analyzes patterns across many conversations. It can surface deals that appear to be at risk, detect competitor mentions, summarize each call, and suggest next steps. Coaching features let managers share clips, give feedback, and compare reps against top performers. Integrations with Salesforce and other CRMs send call data and notes into the customer record so reps spend less time on updates.

item.title: Civitai
item.description:
Civitai is where much of the open-source image generation community meets. Creators upload checkpoints, LoRAs, embeddings, and other add-ons for Stable Diffusion, FLUX, and related models, together with sample images and the prompts used. Others download them to run locally in tools like ComfyUI or Automatic1111, or try them in the browser. Ratings, comments, and example galleries make it easier to judge a model before downloading.

The site offers more than a library. Users can generate images on Civitai’s servers using credits, train their own LoRAs from a set of images, and take part in challenges and bounties that reward creators. Articles and guides share techniques, and a point system pays for the use of the site’s services. It became the unofficial catalog for community-trained styles, characters, and concepts.

item.title: Claap
item.description: Claap targets teams that want fewer live meetings. You can record your screen and camera as a short video, share a link, and let colleagues watch and respond on their own time. The same tool records live calls on Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams, then stores them with a transcript. Comments and reactions can be attached to specific moments, so feedback stays tied to the part of the video it refers to.

item.title: Clari
item.description:
Clari began as a tool to make sales forecasting more reliable. It reads CRM data and signals from email, calendar, and calls to show how deals are progressing, then rolls those into a forecast that managers can inspect by team, region, and stage. The goal is to replace spreadsheet-based forecast calls with data that people trust.

AI helps spot trouble. It scores deals, flags those with stalled activity or missing stakeholders, and suggests actions. Conversation intelligence summarizes calls and highlights risks, and pipeline inspection tools show where coverage is thin. Revenue leaders use it to prepare for board and forecast meetings.

item.title: Claude
item.description: Claude is the AI assistant from Anthropic, a company that focuses on AI safety research. It comes in a few model tiers, with smaller and faster models for quick tasks and larger ones for harder reasoning and coding. People tend to pick it for writing that sounds less formulaic, careful reading of long documents, and code. It is also more willing than some competitors to say it is unsure or to disagree with you, which some users value and others find less accommodating.

item.title: Claude Code
item.description: Claude Code works as an agent on your actual project instead of a suggestion engine in an editor. You start it in a repository from the terminal and describe the task, such as fixing a failing test, adding an endpoint, or upgrading a dependency. It reads the relevant files, makes a plan, edits code across the project, runs tests and other commands, and iterates on the errors. It asks permission for actions that could be risky, and you can review changes as diffs or through git before committing.

item.title: Cleanfeed
item.description:
Cleanfeed lets people record or broadcast audio over the internet without installing software. A host creates a session, guests join by link in a browser, and the platform streams audio with low delay and records each participant on a separate track. It is popular with radio and podcast teams who need dependable quality.

The audio chain is a focus. It offers a noise gate, level controls, and processing options that tidy up voices, plus connections for studio equipment and phone callers. Producers can monitor and route audio, record backups, and download multitrack files. A newer version improves collaboration and integration with video.

item.title: Cleanup.pictures
item.description:
Cleanup.pictures does one thing with minimal effort. Upload a photo, brush over a stranger in the background, a power line, a logo, or a blemish, and the tool removes it and fills the gap with a plausible background. Results come back within seconds and can be downloaded, which makes it a quick fix for product photos, real estate listings, travel pictures, and social media posts.

It works well on simple backgrounds such as sky, grass, walls, and water, and less well when the removed object sits in front of detailed patterns, faces, or text that the model would have to invent. For larger images, a higher-resolution output is available on paid plans. The same kind of inpainting appears in other tools, including Clipdrop, which offers a related cleanup feature, along with Photoshop’s Generative Fill and Remove tool and the Magic Eraser on Google Pixel phones.

item.title: Cleanvoice
item.description: Cleanvoice does one job: it cleans up speech. You upload a podcast episode, interview, or video, and it finds the places where a speaker said “um” or “uh,” paused for too long, made lip smacks or breath sounds, or repeated a word. It removes them and returns a tidier file. Editing these by hand takes a long time, and a one-hour recording can contain hundreds of them, so automating it saves real hours for podcasters and video creators.

item.title: Clickup
item.description: ClickUp tries to be a single home for everything a team does. At its center are tasks that can be shown as lists, boards, calendars, Gantt charts, or timelines, and each task can have subtasks, custom fields, dependencies, and checklists. Around that sit docs, wikis, whiteboards, forms, dashboards, goals, and built-in chat. Teams use it for software sprints, marketing calendars, client projects, and operations, and the same workspace can be shaped differently for each department.

item.title: Clideo
item.description:
Clideo offers simple video tools that run in the browser. A user uploads a clip, picks a tool such as trimming, merging, compressing, resizing, or converting formats, and downloads the result. The pitch is convenience for quick jobs where installing editing software is not worth it.

AI features add some automation. Auto subtitles transcribe speech and add styled captions in many languages, and background removal and other effects help prepare clips for social media. The editor handles basic timeline work, and tools for audio, GIFs, and screen recording are included in the suite.

item.title: ClimaCell
item.description:
Tomorrow.io focuses on weather as a business input. Companies in aviation, logistics, energy, retail, and sports use its platform to get forecasts and alerts tailored to their locations and operations, such as a warning when wind will halt crane operations or when snow will affect deliveries. The goal is to turn weather into decisions, not just data.

It builds its own data sources. The company has launched satellites carrying radar to observe precipitation, which supplements ground sensors and models and helps in regions with limited coverage. AI blends these inputs to make short-range forecasts, and an assistant helps users create alerts and ask questions about conditions. APIs deliver the data into other applications.

item.title: Climate FieldView
item.description:
Climate FieldView helps farmers use their data. With a device plugged into farm equipment, FieldView Drive collects information about planting, applications, and harvest, and the data syncs to the cloud, where farmers view maps of their fields, compare hybrids and practices, and analyze yield. Satellite imagery tracks crop health during the season, and weather data and field notes add context.

Advanced features support planning. Variable-rate prescriptions tell equipment to apply seed and fertilizer at different rates across a field based on zones, which can improve efficiency, and scripts or models estimate the profitability of decisions. Integrations with equipment and other agriculture software reduce manual data transfers. Machine learning supports yield predictions and recommendations.

item.title: Climate TRACE
item.description: Climate TRACE exists because official emissions reporting is slow and incomplete. The coalition combines satellite images, sensor data, and public records and applies machine learning to estimate emissions from individual sources: power plants, steel mills, oil and gas fields, ships, aircraft, cement plants, farms, and more. The result is a global inventory that can be searched by country, sector, or even a single facility, updated more frequently than government reports.

item.title: Clockwise
item.description:
Clockwise worked inside Google Calendar and Slack to protect time for deep work. It looked at a team’s calendars, moved flexible meetings, and combined scattered gaps into longer blocks, aiming to cut the constant switching between tasks that fragments a workday. It could also find meeting times that worked for groups.

The product grew a following among engineering and product teams, and added AI scheduling features and a way to plan work around priorities. The company ended the service and the team joined Salesforce, where they work on AI agents. The product itself did not move over.

item.title: Coda AI
item.description:
Coda reimagines the document as something that can behave like an app. A Coda doc can contain text, tables, buttons, and automations, so a team can build a project tracker, a wiki, a CRM, or a planning tool in the same document where they write. Formulas, similar to those in spreadsheets, connect data across the doc, and Packs integrate with outside services such as Slack, Jira, and Google Calendar.

AI features run through the platform. Coda AI can summarize documents, draft text, fill table columns with generated content, categorize and extract information, and answer questions about the contents of a doc. AI blocks and agents can be placed in workflows to automate tasks. The company joined Grammarly, which has taken the name Superhuman, and its tools are being combined with Grammarly’s writing assistant and the Superhuman email app.

item.title: Codeium
item.description: Codeium started as a free alternative to GitHub Copilot, offering code completion and chat in more than 40 editors, among them VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Vim, and Neovim. Its free individual tier and wide editor support earned it a large user base among developers who did not want to pay for a coding assistant or switch editors. It added features such as natural-language code search, in-editor chat, and support for dozens of programming languages.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit acts as a first reviewer. When a developer opens a pull request, it reads the diff along with surrounding code, writes a summary of the change, and leaves comments on potential bugs, missing tests, security concerns, and style. Developers can reply to its comments and ask it to explain or fix things, so the review becomes a conversation.

Configuration lets teams set rules and instructions in plain language so the review follows their standards. It learns from feedback, and can run linters and security scanners as part of the review. IDE and command line versions bring review earlier, before a pull request is opened.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit gives every pull request a quick first review. When a developer opens a pull request, it summarizes the change, walks through the files, and leaves comments on potential bugs, security problems, performance concerns, and deviations from team conventions. It can also suggest fixes that developers apply with a click and answer questions in the comments, acting like a tireless reviewer available at any hour.

It improves with use. CodeRabbit learns from how reviewers respond to its suggestions and from guidelines the team defines, so comments become more relevant over time. It runs linters and security scanners as part of its review, can use context from the wider codebase, and has an IDE and command-line version for reviewing before code is pushed. It integrates with issue trackers to check that changes match requirements.

item.title: Codiga
item.description:
Codiga offered real-time code analysis inside the editor. Its plugins for VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and other tools scanned code as you typed for security vulnerabilities, bugs, and violations of coding standards, and a rules engine let teams write their own checks. It also provided a code snippet assistant and, later, AI-based suggestions, and integrated with Git platforms to review pull requests automatically.

The company was acquired by Datadog, which wanted to bring code analysis into its observability and security platform. Codiga’s standalone products were shut down shortly afterward, with refunds for paid subscribers, and the team joined Datadog. The static analysis engine and its rules now underpin Datadog Code Security, and the analyzer is available as open source.

item.title: Colossyan
item.description: Colossyan targets companies that need a lot of video for learning and communication but do not want to film each one. You type or paste a script, or upload a document or slides and have it converted, choose an AI presenter and voice, and Colossyan produces a video. Editing works like slides, with scenes, text, images, and screen recordings, and changing the script means regenerating the video instead of reshooting.

item.title: ComfyUI
item.description: ComfyUI gives you precise control over generative AI by showing the whole pipeline. Instead of a prompt box and a button, you assemble a graph: load a model, encode a prompt, set up a sampler, add LoRAs or ControlNet for guidance, upscale, and save. Each step is a node you can inspect and rewire. It started with Stable Diffusion and now supports many image, video, and audio models, including FLUX, so new models are often usable in ComfyUI first.

item.title: Compass
item.description:
Compass is a brokerage that positions itself as a technology company. Its agents use a platform that combines a customer relationship manager, marketing tools for listings, market data, and transaction management in one place. Homebuyers and sellers use the site and app to search listings, see market trends, and work with an agent, and the tools are free to consumers because the company earns money through commissions on sales.

Technology supports the agent workflow. The platform helps with pricing recommendations, creates marketing materials such as brochures and social posts, tracks leads and client conversations, and organizes documents and deadlines through a deal. AI features assist with drafting listing descriptions, summarizing client interactions, and surfacing homes or clients to contact. The company has also tested private listings strategies for sellers.

item.title: Compose AI
item.description:
Compose AI works wherever you type in Chrome. As you write an email or a message, it suggests the next words or sentence, which you accept with a keystroke, similar to code completion in a programming editor. It can also draft whole replies, rewrite text in a different tone, and fix grammar, with a menu of shortcuts for common tasks.

The product came from a startup that focused on autocomplete for writing, and later added generative features that call large language models for longer tasks. It is intended to save keystrokes on repetitive writing such as emails, support replies, and social posts, and to reduce the effort of starting a draft. A free tier covers basic use, with paid plans for more generations and features.

item.title: Composio
item.description:
Composio is an integration layer for AI agents. Agents need to take actions in other software, which means handling authentication and API details for each service. Composio supplies a catalog of connectors that handle sign-in flows and expose actions in a form models can call, so a developer can give an agent access to many apps with a few lines of code.

It works with agent frameworks and model providers, supports the Model Context Protocol, and manages user authorization so that agents act on behalf of each end user. Tools for monitoring let developers see what actions agents took, and permissions limit what an agent can do.

item.title: Consensus
item.description: Consensus searches a large database of academic papers instead of the open web. You ask a question in plain language, such as whether a supplement improves sleep, and it returns an answer built from the studies it finds, with each claim linked to its source. For yes-or-no questions, the Consensus Meter shows how the papers split between yes, no, and mixed results. The result is a faster way to see what the evidence says without reading dozens of abstracts.

item.title: Content at Scale
item.description:
Content at Scale launched as a tool for generating complete blog posts. You enter a keyword, a URL, or a video, and the system researches the topic and writes a long article designed to read naturally, with sections, headings, and optimization for search. It was marketed on producing content that would pass AI detection and be useful to readers, which made it popular with SEO agencies and publishers.

The company has rebranded to BrandWell and widened its offering. It now describes a platform for brand growth that includes keyword research, content planning, optimization, and generation, with the long-form writer continuing as one of its core tools. Existing customers kept their accounts, and the older name may still appear on some pages or in billing.

item.title: ContentStudio
item.description:
ContentStudio combines content discovery, creation, and publishing. Users find trending topics and articles, curate and share them, write posts with an AI assistant, and schedule to networks such as Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, TikTok, and WordPress blogs. A calendar shows what is planned across channels.

Features for teams and agencies include approval workflows, client management, white-label reports, and analytics on performance. The AI writer generates captions, hashtags, and blog drafts, and image tools help create visuals. Social inbox features centralize replies and comments.

item.title: Conversica
item.description:
Conversica automates the follow-up that sales teams often drop. When a lead comes in, the AI assistant sends personalized messages, reads replies, answers questions, and tries to book a meeting. If a prospect does not respond, it continues with a sequence of nudges, which keeps leads from going cold.

The assistants are used in industries such as automotive, education, software, and financial services, where large volumes of inquiries arrive. Conversation data flows into the CRM, so salespeople see which leads are qualified and what was said. The company has added generative AI to make conversations more natural.

item.title: Copy.ai
item.description:
Copy.ai began as one of the first popular AI copywriting tools. Users choose a template or write a prompt, and the tool generates headlines, product descriptions, email sequences, ads, and social captions. A brand voice feature helps keep the tone consistent.

The product later shifted toward workflows for go-to-market teams. Marketers and sales teams can chain steps that research accounts, draft outreach, and produce content at scale, using multiple language models. Chat and knowledge features let the AI draw on company information.

item.title: Copy.ai
item.description:
Copy.ai started in the first wave of AI writing tools. You picked a template, such as a product description, email, or social caption, answered a few prompts, and got several drafts to edit. It was popular with marketers and small businesses who needed a lot of copy quickly. Over time it moved away from one-off text generation and toward automating sales and marketing processes.

Its later product centered on workflows. A team could chain steps together, for example researching an account, pulling in data, drafting outreach, and writing a CRM update, and let AI agents run the sequence on a schedule or trigger. A data layer called Tables kept the inputs organized, and the aim was to replace manual go-to-market busywork with repeatable automations rather than just generating paragraphs.

item.title: Copyleaks
item.description:
Copyleaks checks text for originality. It compares documents against web pages, publications, and its own databases to find copied passages, and it also estimates whether text was written by an AI model. Schools, publishers, and businesses use it to check student work, submissions, and content.

It supports many languages and file types, and integrates with learning management systems so teachers can scan assignments in their usual workflow. Reports show matched sources and highlight text flagged as likely AI-written. Additional tools cover code plagiarism and a writing assistant.

item.title: CoreWeave
item.description:
CoreWeave began as a company mining cryptocurrency and turned its GPU capacity into a cloud for AI. Customers rent clusters of NVIDIA GPUs for training and running models, with networking and storage built for large workloads. Because it specializes, it can often deploy new GPU generations quickly.

The platform runs on Kubernetes and offers managed services for training, inference, and storage. Major AI labs and big technology companies have signed large contracts, and the company has built or leased data centers around the world. It acquired Weights & Biases to add developer tooling to its infrastructure.

item.title: Coursera
item.description:
Coursera partners with universities and companies to offer online learning at scale. Learners can take individual courses, follow multi-course specializations and professional certificates from names like Google, IBM, and Meta, or enroll in full online degrees. Material combines video lectures, readings, quizzes, and graded assignments, and many courses can be audited for free. Completed programs earn certificates that people add to resumes and LinkedIn.

AI has become part of the platform. A learning assistant answers questions about course content, gives feedback, and helps with practice, and tools help instructors and organizations build and translate courses faster. Skills-based recommendations suggest what to learn next based on your goals. The platform also offers business and government offerings, where employers assign programs and track progress.

item.title: Coze
item.description:
Coze lets non-programmers build conversational agents. In its editor, you describe the bot’s role and behavior, choose a language model, and attach tools: plugins for web search, image generation, and other services, plus knowledge bases that hold your documents. Visual workflows chain steps together for more complex tasks, and memory features let a bot recall details about users. A store lets creators share and discover bots built by others.

Publishing is flexible. A finished agent can be deployed to messaging apps and chat platforms, embedded on a website, or exposed through an API, which makes it practical for customer support, community bots, personal assistants, and internal tools. ByteDance has also released parts of the platform as open source for those who want to run it themselves, and offers separate editions for different regions.

item.title: Craft Docs
item.description: Craft aims to make notes and documents that look good. It works as a block-based editor where text, images, tables, and cards live in nested pages that you can reorganize easily. Native apps for Mac, iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch are fast and polished, with offline support, and there is also a web and Windows version. Daily notes and tasks cover personal organization, and Spaces and collections keep larger projects tidy.

item.title: Craiyon
item.description:
Craiyon began as DALL-E mini, an open-source experiment that went viral for producing odd, low-resolution images from text prompts. It was one of the first image generators many people tried, and it popularized the idea that anyone could make pictures with words. The site then rebranded as Craiyon and kept its low barrier to entry: open the page, type a prompt, and wait for the results.

The quality has improved with newer models, and Craiyon now produces more detailed images in several styles, including photos, illustrations, and drawings. Paid plans remove ads, speed up generation, and add features such as faster queues, higher resolution, and a private mode. The tool is positioned for casual use, like quick illustrations, memes, and idea sketches, instead of professional production.

item.title: CrewAI
item.description: CrewAI uses the metaphor of a team. You create agents with specific roles, such as researcher, writer, and reviewer, give each a goal and a set of tools, and assign tasks. The agents work in sequence or in parallel, passing results to one another, and a manager can coordinate them. This structure suits tasks that break down naturally into steps handled by different specialists, like market research reports or content pipelines.

item.title: Crimson Hexagon
item.description: Crimson Hexagon was a consumer insights company that analyzed social media, news, forums, and review data at large scale. It was known for its ForSight platform and for machine learning that classified posts by sentiment and topic with accuracy that researchers could tune. Market researchers, agencies, and brands used it to track what people said about products and campaigns, and its archive of historical social data was a draw for studying trends over time.

item.title: Crunchbase
item.description:
Crunchbase is a widely used database about startups and private companies. Users look up a company to see its founders, funding history, investors, and news, or search for companies by industry, location, and stage. Investors, salespeople, and researchers use it to find targets and track activity.

Predictive features add forward-looking signals. AI models estimate which companies are likely to raise money, grow, or be acquired, and alerts notify users when relevant events happen. Lists and integrations send data into CRMs for prospecting.

item.title: Culture Amp
item.description:
Culture Amp helps companies listen to employees. HR teams run engagement, onboarding, and exit surveys, analyze the results by team and demographic group, and compare against benchmarks from other organizations. Dashboards point out areas where scores are low and what drives them.

The platform also covers performance and development, with review cycles, goal tracking, and feedback. AI helps by summarizing open-ended comments into themes, drafting review text, and recommending actions to managers, which saves analysts days of reading. An assistant answers questions about results.

item.title: Cursor
item.description: Cursor started as a fork of Visual Studio Code, so the interface, extensions, and keybindings are familiar to anyone who has used VS Code. The difference is that AI is part of the editor rather than an add-on. It predicts your next edit, not just the next token, so a rename or a repeated change can often be applied with a single tab press. You can also select code and ask for a rewrite, or chat with a model that has indexed the whole repository and can answer questions about files you have not opened.

item.title: Cursor Composer
item.description: Composer was Cursor’s answer to a basic limit of early AI coding tools, which could suggest a line or edit one file but struggled with changes that touched several. You describe a feature or refactor, and Composer works out which files need to change, writes the edits, and shows them as diffs for you to accept or reject. It can create new files, update imports, and keep related code consistent. The feature later evolved into Cursor’s agent, which also runs commands and fixes its own errors.

item.title: D-ID
item.description:
D-ID became known for animating still photos. You upload a portrait and add a script or audio, and the platform produces a video in which the person appears to speak, with lip movement and facial expressions. That idea grew into a full avatar platform: a studio where you create presenters, choose voices and languages, and generate videos for training, marketing, and customer communication.

Beyond videos, D-ID provides tools for interactive use. An API lets developers generate talking avatars in their own applications, and real-time agents combine an avatar, a language model, and a voice so that a digital person can hold a conversation on a website or kiosk. The company also works on privacy technology, with its origins in tools that protect faces from recognition systems.

item.title: Dark Sky
item.description:
Dark Sky changed expectations for weather apps. Using radar data and machine learning, it predicted when rain or snow would start and stop at your exact location, with messages such as light rain starting in 10 minutes. That focus on the next hour, rather than a general daily forecast, made it popular with people who walk, run, or commute, and its design was clean and quick to read.

It also offered an API that thousands of apps and websites used for weather data. Developers valued its simple interface and detailed forecasts, which made it a common building block in other products. Apple acquired the company, integrated its technology into Apple Weather, and then retired the Dark Sky app and its API.

item.title: DataRobot
item.description:
DataRobot pioneered automated machine learning. A data team uploads a dataset, and the platform tries many algorithms and feature combinations, ranks them, and explains the best models, which lowers the barrier to building predictive models for tasks such as churn, demand, and risk. It also handles deployment and monitoring, tracking model accuracy and drift once models are live.

The company has pivoted toward generative AI and agents. Its platform now helps companies build and run AI agents and applications, with governance features such as documentation, bias checks, approvals, and audit trails that matter in industries such as banking, insurance, and healthcare. It can run in the cloud or on a company’s own infrastructure and integrates with major cloud providers and data platforms.

item.title: dbt Cloud
item.description:
dbt, short for data build tool, became the standard way to transform raw data inside a warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks. Analysts write SQL select statements, define dependencies among them, and dbt builds tables and views in the right order, with version control, testing, and documentation. This brings software engineering practices like code review and continuous integration to analytics work.

dbt Cloud is the hosted product from dbt Labs. It provides a browser-based IDE, job scheduling, CI that tests changes before they reach production, a data catalog with lineage, and a semantic layer that defines metrics once for use across BI tools. AI features help generate models, tests, and documentation, and answer questions about the project, which speeds up repetitive tasks.

item.title: Decktopus
item.description: Decktopus is built for people who need a presentation quickly. You enter a topic or a short brief, answer a few questions about the audience and goal, and the AI produces an outline and a deck of designed slides with suggested images and speaker notes. You then edit the text and layout in a drag-and-drop editor. It also offers templates for pitches, reports, and sales decks, and a brand kit for colors and logos.

item.title: DeepL
item.description:
DeepL built its reputation on translations that read more naturally than many competitors, especially for European languages. You paste text or upload a document, such as a Word file, PDF, or PowerPoint, and get a translation that keeps the formatting. Options let you choose formal or informal tone, add glossaries for specific terms, and see alternative wordings for phrases.

The product has expanded into a broader language platform. DeepL Write improves and rephrases text in the same language, DeepL Voice translates live conversations and meetings, and browser extensions and desktop apps translate as you work. An API serves developers and enterprises, and newer agent features automate tasks. Business plans add data security, which promises that texts are not used for training, plus team glossaries.

item.title: Demandbase
item.description:
Demandbase focuses on selling to companies rather than individuals. It builds a view of target accounts from first-party and third-party data, including website visits, content use, and intent signals showing which accounts are researching a topic. Marketing and sales teams see which accounts are heating up and who within them is involved.

The platform acts on those signals. Advertising features serve targeted ads to the buying committee at chosen accounts, sales tools alert reps when accounts show interest, and orchestration coordinates campaigns across channels. AI helps score accounts, predict fit, and recommend actions, and an assistant answers questions about account data.

item.title: Descript
item.description:
Descript changed podcast editing by turning audio into text. After you record or import an episode, it transcribes it, and you cut, move, and delete sections by editing the words, which is much faster than working on waveforms. Filler words and long pauses can be removed in bulk, and multitrack editing, music, and effects are available for more polished shows.

Recording and polishing tools are built in. Remote recording captures guests in high quality, Studio Sound improves voice clarity and reduces noise, and an Overdub feature can fix mistakes with a synthetic version of your voice. AI assistants draft titles, descriptions, and show notes, suggest chapters, and generate clips and audiograms for social media. Episodes can be published to hosting platforms or exported.

item.title: Descript
item.description:
Descript changed how many people edit podcasts and videos. After recording, Descript transcribes the audio, and deleting a word from the transcript cuts it from the media. That makes editing feel like working in a document, which is friendlier for people without video editing experience.

AI tools extend the idea. Studio Sound improves audio quality in one click, filler word removal cleans speech, eye contact correction adjusts gaze, and the underlord assistant performs edits from instructions. Voice cloning lets you fix a word by typing it, and text can drive screen recording, multi-track editing, and clips for social media.

item.title: Descript
item.description: Descript changed how many people edit audio and video. You upload a recording, it produces a transcript, and you cut, rearrange, and delete the media by editing the text like a document. Removing a sentence in the transcript removes it from the recording. For podcasts, interviews, tutorials, and talking-head videos, that is much faster than working on a waveform, and people who have never used an editor can pick it up quickly.

item.title: Descript Studio Sound
item.description:
Studio Sound targets the common problem of recording in imperfect spaces. Apply it to a clip in Descript, and the AI removes noise, reduces echo and reverb, and evens out the voice, making recordings made on a laptop or phone sound much more professional. It works on a whole project or a selected portion and has an intensity setting, so you can balance cleanup against natural sound.

It is built into Descript’s editing workflow, so you can clean audio while editing the transcript, and it works on both audio and video projects. Podcasters, interviewers, educators, and video creators use it to rescue recordings from noisy environments. It can be combined with other features in Descript, such as filler word removal and eye contact correction for video.

item.title: Devv.ai
item.description: Devv.ai was built as a search tool for programmers, positioned between a traditional search engine and a chatbot. You ask a technical question, such as how to configure a library or why an error occurs, and it searches documentation, GitHub repositories, and developer discussions and then writes an answer with sources. Linking to sources helps you verify the answer, which matters because chatbots can invent APIs or settings that do not exist.

item.title: Dify
item.description: Dify gives teams a visual way to build AI applications without writing everything from scratch. In its workflow editor, you connect blocks for models, prompts, knowledge retrieval, code, conditions, and tool calls to create chatbots, agents, and automations. Knowledge pipelines ingest documents, split and index them, and let the application answer questions from your own data. You can test and debug each run, then publish the app as a web interface or API.

item.title: Dimensions
item.description:
Dimensions connects different kinds of research outputs. Instead of searching only for papers, users can see how a grant led to publications, which patents cite a study, and whether a trial or policy document refers to it. The linked structure helps trace the path from funding to impact.

Institutions, funders, and researchers use it for several purposes. Universities benchmark their output, funders track results of the grants they award, and companies look for experts and emerging fields. AI features summarize results, help with literature searches, and surface connections, and APIs let organizations pull data into their own systems.

item.title: DocuSign AI
item.description:
Docusign made electronic signatures routine. Senders upload a document, specify signers and fields, and recipients sign on any device, with an audit trail and legal validity in many countries. It’s used for sales contracts, HR paperwork, real estate, and any agreement that once needed a pen, and it integrates with Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and many business systems.

The company has expanded to manage the whole agreement lifecycle. Its Intelligent Agreement Management platform includes tools to prepare and negotiate agreements, a repository that stores them, and AI that reads contracts to extract terms such as renewal dates, obligations, and parties. Its AI can summarize documents, answer questions about a contract portfolio, and flag risks, and workflow tools automate steps such as approvals and routing.

item.title: Dolby.io
item.description:
Dolby.io brings Dolby’s audio expertise to developers as web services. A developer sends an audio or video file and receives a processed version: cleaner speech, reduced background noise, balanced loudness, or improved dialogue. These APIs fit podcast tools, video platforms, and conferencing products.

Other parts of the platform focus on real-time streaming. Millicast delivers low-latency video to large audiences, which suits live events, interactive broadcasts, and remote production. Analysis and transcoding APIs help prepare content for different devices.

item.title: Domo AI
item.description:
Domo aims to put an organization’s data in one place. It connects to hundreds of sources, from databases and spreadsheets to marketing and finance platforms, and lets users clean and combine data and then build dashboards and reports. Business users can view metrics on the web or mobile and set alerts, and developers can build custom apps on top of the data.

AI is built through the product. Users can ask questions in natural language and receive charts and answers, models can forecast and detect anomalies, and AI agents and workflows can automate tasks, such as summarizing reports or triggering actions when numbers change. Domo also lets companies connect their own models, and offers governance features for data access.

item.title: DoNotPay
item.description:
DoNotPay started by helping people contest parking tickets and grew into an app for dealing with the small annoyances of consumer life. Its tools help users write letters and fill out forms to dispute charges, cancel unwanted subscriptions, request refunds, and complain to companies and agencies. The idea is that many of these tasks are tedious and intimidating, and a template-driven assistant can save people time and money.

The company’s marketing as the world’s first robot lawyer caused trouble. The Federal Trade Commission alleged that the service did not perform as well as a human lawyer and did not have the testing to back its claims. A final order barred DoNotPay from making that kind of claim without evidence and required it to pay a fine and notify affected customers. The case is often cited as a warning about overstating what AI can do in legal matters.

item.title: Dovetail
item.description:
Dovetail gives research teams a home for customer feedback. Researchers upload interviews and other data, and the platform transcribes recordings, lets them highlight key quotes, and organizes everything so insights can be found later. Teams build a searchable repository instead of losing findings in slide decks.

AI shortens the analysis step. It tags content automatically, groups related feedback into themes, summarizes sessions, and answers questions across a body of research. Reports and shareable highlights help researchers communicate with product teams and executives, and integrations pull in data from support and survey tools.

item.title: Dream by WOMBO
item.description: Dream by WOMBO is aimed at casual creators who want to see their ideas as art without learning prompt techniques. You type a phrase, pick a style such as oil painting, anime, fantasy, or neon, and the app returns an image in a few seconds. The style menu does much of the work that detailed prompts would do in other tools, which makes it approachable on a phone. It is popular for profile pictures, wallpapers, and quick social posts.

item.title: DreamBox Learning
item.description: DreamBox Math is designed to give every student lessons at the right level. As a child works through interactive, game-based problems, the software tracks not only whether answers are correct but also how the child solves them: the strategies used, the time taken, and the kinds of mistakes made. It uses that information to adjust the next activity, moving ahead when the student is ready and revisiting ideas when they are shaky.

item.title: Duolingo
item.description:
Duolingo made language learning feel like a game. Lessons take a few minutes and mix translation, matching, listening, and speaking exercises. Streaks, experience points, and leagues reward consistency, and the friendly design and persistent reminders turned it into one of the most used education apps in the world. Courses cover languages from Spanish and French to Japanese, Korean, and smaller options, and it also offers math, music, and chess.

AI is a growing part of the product. A paid tier called Max includes features such as explanations of why an answer was right or wrong and role-play conversations with an AI character, and video call practice lets learners speak with an animated character. The company also uses AI to generate and personalize lesson content, which has been controversial among some users and staff who worry about quality and jobs.

item.title: Durable
item.description:
Durable promises a website with minimal effort. You tell it the kind of business you run and where you are, and it builds a site with pages, copy, images, and a layout in under a minute, which you can then edit with simple controls. It’s aimed at freelancers and local service businesses, such as plumbers, photographers, and consultants, who need an online presence quickly.

Beyond the site, Durable includes small-business tools. A built-in CRM tracks leads and customers, an invoicing feature handles billing, and AI assistants help write blog posts, social content, and marketing copy. It offers hosting and a custom domain, and basic analytics. Everything lives in one account, so owners avoid piecing together several services.

item.title: Dynamic Yield
item.description:
Dynamic Yield helps businesses show each customer the content most likely to interest them. It collects behavior data from web, mobile, and email channels, builds profiles and segments, and uses machine learning to choose which products, banners, or messages to show. Retailers use it for recommendations like customers also bought, personalized homepages, and tailored promotions.

The platform also covers testing and optimization. Teams run experiments to compare versions of pages, with statistics to determine winners, and use triggers such as exit intent to present timely offers. Integrations connect with e-commerce platforms, customer data platforms, and marketing tools, and AI features suggest audiences and automate decisions. It supports use in industries including retail, travel, banking, and media.

item.title: E2B
item.description:
E2B gives AI agents a safe computer. When a language model writes code, running it directly on a server is risky. E2B creates an isolated sandbox in the cloud, executes the code, returns the output and files, and shuts it down. Startup is fast enough to be used inside an agent loop.

Developers use its SDKs for Python and JavaScript to start sandboxes, run commands, read and write files, and stream results. It supports data analysis agents, coding assistants, and tools that need browsers or desktops, and templates define the environment. The core is open source and can be self-hosted.

item.title: Elai.io
item.description:
Elai.io is aimed at people who need a presenter video without filming. A user picks from a library of avatars, enters a script or imports a document, selects a voice and language, and the platform produces a video of the avatar speaking. Backgrounds, text, and media can be added in a slide-like editor.

Typical uses are training videos, product explainers, and marketing content, and the ability to translate into many languages helps localize quickly. Custom avatars can be created from a person’s footage. Features such as converting articles or links into videos speed up content creation.

item.title: ElevenLabs
item.description:
ElevenLabs is known for natural-sounding synthetic speech. Users type text and choose a voice, or clone a voice from a sample, and get audio that carries intonation and emotion. The platform supports dozens of languages and accents and offers a library of voices.

Its products now span several uses. Dubbing translates video into other languages while keeping the speaker’s voice, audiobook and narration tools produce long-form audio, and a conversational agent platform builds voice assistants that talk with customers in real time. Music and sound effect generation, plus speech to text, round out the suite. An API lets developers embed these features.

item.title: ElevenLabs
item.description: ElevenLabs is best known for text-to-speech that sounds like a person rather than a robot. You paste in a script, choose a voice from a large library or make your own, and the tool reads it with natural pacing and emotion. The same voice can speak dozens of languages, which makes it a popular option for audiobooks, YouTube narration, e-learning, game characters, and accessibility. Voice cloning builds a copy of a voice from a recording, and there are safeguards around it: you are meant to have the speaker’s permission, and some features require identity checks.

item.title: ElevenLabs Sound Effects
item.description:
ElevenLabs Sound Effects creates audio from a sentence. You describe the sound you need, such as a door creaking in an empty house or a crowd cheering in a stadium, and the model generates several options in seconds, which you can adjust for length and download. This helps video editors, game developers, podcasters, and filmmakers who otherwise search libraries for the right clip or record effects themselves.

The company also offers a Voice Isolator that separates speech from background noise and music, helping clean up interviews and field recordings. These tools fit alongside ElevenLabs’ text-to-speech, dubbing, and music features, so a creator can produce a full soundtrack in one place. An API allows developers to generate effects inside apps and games.

item.title: Elicit
item.description:
Elicit helps researchers move through academic literature faster. A user asks a research question, and Elicit searches a large database of papers, presents relevant results, and extracts details such as sample size, methods, and outcomes into a table. Seeing structured comparisons across studies is much quicker than reading each paper in full.

Additional tools support systematic review work. Users can screen papers against criteria, summarize findings, and build reports, with citations tied to the passages in each paper so claims can be checked. It is used by students, academics, and professionals in evidence-based fields.

item.title: Elicit
item.description: Elicit is built for people who need to work through a large body of research. You ask a research question, and it finds relevant papers and shows a table with key details such as the study design, sample size, and results. You can add columns for the things you care about, and Elicit extracts the answers from each paper, so a review that might take days of reading can be started in an afternoon. Each extracted point links back to the passage in the paper it came from.

item.title: Eraser
item.description:
Eraser is built around engineers’ diagrams. Users can write diagrams as code in a simple syntax, draw them visually, or describe them in plain language and let AI generate the first version. The result stays editable, with a clean style that looks good in documentation and design reviews.

The product also supports documents. Eraser has a docs editor where diagrams sit alongside text for design documents and runbooks, and integrations with GitHub allow diagrams to be generated from a repository and kept in sync. Teams share and comment on documents in real time.

item.title: Exa AI
item.description: Exa, formerly Metaphor, rethinks search for machines instead of people. Where a traditional engine matches keywords, Exa uses neural embeddings to find pages that are semantically similar to a query, even when they do not share words. You can search with natural-language descriptions, such as a list of startups building a specific kind of robot, and it returns results that match the idea. It can also take a link and find similar pages.

item.title: Expensify
item.description:
Expensify is known for making expense reports less painful. Employees photograph receipts or forward them by email, SmartScan extracts the merchant, date, and amount, and the app builds a report for submission. Managers approve in the app, and approved expenses sync to accounting software.

Other features cover company spending. The Expensify Card gives employees corporate cards with real-time receipts matching, policies flag out-of-bounds expenses automatically, and mileage tracking and per diems handle travel. AI helps categorize spending and spot policy issues.

item.title: Explainpaper
item.description: Explainpaper targets a familiar frustration: academic papers are dense and full of jargon. You upload a PDF, select the sentence, equation, or paragraph you do not understand, and the tool gives a plain-language explanation. You can adjust the level, from a lay audience to an expert, and ask follow-up questions about the paper. It was popular with students and curious readers who wanted to follow a paper outside their own field.

item.title: Factorial
item.description:
Factorial gathers HR tasks in one system. Companies store employee records, track attendance and time off, manage documents and contracts, run performance reviews, and handle recruiting and onboarding. Payroll is offered in several countries, and integrations connect with accounting and communication tools.

AI helps with administrative work. It can draft job descriptions and offer letters, answer employee questions about policies, and speed up payroll preparation. Reports give managers a view of headcount and absence.

item.title: FarmLogs
item.description:
FarmLogs began as a way for farmers to keep records digitally instead of in notebooks. Growers could map their fields, log planting, spraying, and harvest activities, track inputs and costs, and see weather and satellite imagery for each field. The aim was to make it easier to understand what was working in a season, to meet record-keeping requirements, and to share information with advisors and landlords.

The product became part of Bushel, a company that provides software for grain buyers, farmers, and the supply chain. Under the name Bushel Farm, it connects farmers with grain markets and elevators, shows contract and delivery information, and supports tools for tracking grain inventory. Data from fields and grain marketing is brought into one view, and analytics help evaluate profitability.

item.title: Fashwell
item.description:
Fashwell works on a persistent problem in online retail: product data is often incomplete or inconsistent. Its AI looks at product photos and automatically identifies attributes such as category, color, pattern, shape, neckline, and material, creating detailed, standardized tags. Those tags help retailers organize catalogs, improve search, and power filters that match how customers describe items.

The same technology supports discovery features. Visual search lets shoppers find similar items from an image, recommendation systems suggest products that match a style, and outfit and style-matching tools help shoppers complete a look. Retailers use it to save the effort of manual tagging across thousands of items and to improve the consistency of information across channels.

item.title: Fathom
item.description: Fathom is known for making meeting notes free. It joins your Zoom, Google Meet, or Microsoft Teams calls, records them, and creates a transcript in real time. You can highlight important moments during the call with a click, and within seconds of the meeting ending, it produces a summary with decisions, action items, and key points that you can share. The free plan includes unlimited recordings and transcripts, which set it apart from competitors that cap free use.

item.title: Feedzai
item.description:
Feedzai provides real-time fraud detection for banks, card issuers, and payment companies. Its models look at each transaction along with customer and device behavior and decide in milliseconds whether to approve, block, or send it for review. Flagging account takeover, card fraud, and scams quickly limits losses.

The platform also covers anti-money laundering and customer risk, combining signals from different parts of a bank in a single view. Case management tools help investigators work alerts, and explainability features show why a decision was made, which matters to regulators. Newer work addresses authorized scams where customers are tricked into sending money.

item.title: Fellow
item.description:
Fellow helps teams run better meetings. Before a meeting, it provides shared agendas and templates for one-on-ones, team meetings, and client calls. During the meeting, an AI notetaker records and transcribes, capturing decisions and action items automatically. Afterward, summaries and tasks are sent to attendees.

The platform keeps a record of conversations over time, which suits managers who run recurring one-on-ones. Integrations connect with calendars, Slack, Zoom, Teams, and project tools. AI features answer questions across past meetings and draft follow-up messages. Feedback tools support regular check-ins and performance conversations.

item.title: Figma
item.description: Figma is where a lot of software gets designed before anyone writes code. It runs in the browser, so designers, product managers, engineers, and writers can open the same file at once, leave comments, and watch changes appear live. That ended the old habit of emailing design files back and forth. Its core strengths are vector editing, Auto Layout for components that resize correctly, and shared libraries that keep colors, type, and buttons consistent across a whole product.

item.title: Filmora AI
item.description:
Filmora sits between simple phone apps and professional suites. It offers a timeline editor with effects, titles, transitions, and a large library of templates and stock assets, with a design aimed at beginners and hobbyists.

AI features automate tedious work. Smart cutout removes backgrounds from video, noise removal cleans audio, speech-to-text creates captions, and a text-based editor lets users cut by editing the transcript. Generative tools add music, images, and effects.

item.title: Fireflies.ai
item.description: Fireflies sends a bot into your meetings, usually named Fred, that records the call and creates a transcript with speaker labels. After the meeting, it produces a summary with action items and key topics, and posts them where your team works. Every meeting becomes searchable text, so you can find what a customer said last month or when a decision was made. It supports dozens of languages and works with the main video call platforms and uploaded recordings.

item.title: Fireworks AI
item.description:
Fireworks AI focuses on serving open models efficiently. Developers call popular open-weight language, vision, image, and speech models through an API compatible with OpenAI’s format, and the platform’s optimized inference engine delivers low latency and high throughput. Many companies use it to run models at a lower cost than closed alternatives and to maintain control over which models they use.

The platform goes beyond hosting. It supports fine-tuning on a company’s data, including reinforcement learning methods, deploys custom models, and handles structured outputs and function calling for building agents. Dedicated deployments offer reserved capacity for steady workloads, and features such as batch processing reduce cost for non-urgent jobs. It runs in the cloud, with enterprise options for security and compliance.

item.title: Fivetran
item.description:
Fivetran handles the extract and load steps of data pipelines. A team connects sources such as SaaS applications, databases, and files, picks a destination warehouse, and Fivetran keeps the data synced, adapting automatically when source schemas change. This saves engineers from building and maintaining custom connectors.

The company merged with dbt Labs, the maker of the popular transformation tool, bringing loading and transformation together under one roof. Related products include a metadata and governance layer, and tools that prepare data for AI agents. Features for monitoring, anomaly detection, and lineage help teams trust their data.

item.title: FlexClip
item.description:
FlexClip is a browser-based video maker for people without editing experience. You start from a template or a blank timeline, drop in clips, images, text, and music from its stock library, and trim and arrange them with drag and drop. It exports in common formats and sizes for social platforms, and includes screen and webcam recording for tutorials. It is used by small businesses, teachers, and social media managers.

AI features speed up production. Text-to-video builds a draft from a script or idea, an AI script writer drafts the narration, and auto subtitles transcribe speech and add captions in many languages. Background removal for video, text-to-speech voiceovers, and AI image generation fill other gaps. Some features turn a blog post or product page into a video, which marketers use for repurposing content.

item.title: Flick AI
item.description:
Flick targets people who manage social media without a large team. It combines content planning with AI writing: you can brainstorm ideas, generate captions and post drafts in your own style, and organize them on a calendar before scheduling. A hashtag tool suggests relevant tags, and an analytics view helps you see what performs well.

An AI assistant trained on your past content tries to match your tone and topics, so drafts need less editing than generic output. The platform supports multiple networks, including Instagram, LinkedIn, and TikTok, and offers collaboration features for agencies or small teams to review and approve content. Prompts and templates help with common formats such as carousels and short videos.

item.title: Fliki
item.description:
Fliki turns written content into video. A user pastes a script, links an article, or writes a prompt, and the tool splits it into scenes, picks visuals from a stock library or generated media, and adds narration with a synthetic voice. The editor allows swapping clips, adjusting text, and changing voices.

A big draw is the range of voices and languages, which lets creators produce the same video in several markets. Avatars and voice cloning are available, and text to speech is offered as a standalone product for narration and audio. Marketers, educators, and YouTubers use it to repurpose content.

item.title: Flowise
item.description:
Flowise lets people assemble AI applications visually. In its canvas, you connect nodes representing models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools into a flow, test it in a chat window, and expose it through an API or an embedded widget. It started as a visual layer over LangChain and LlamaIndex and has grown to include agent flows with branching, loops, and human approval steps.

Typical uses include chatbots that answer from company documents, customer support assistants, and agents that call APIs and tools. It supports many model providers, including local models through Ollama, and many vector databases, which gives teams a choice about where data and compute live. Because it is open source, it can be self-hosted, and the project has a strong community and many templates.

item.title: FlutterFlow
item.description: FlutterFlow combines the speed of a visual builder with real code. You design screens by dragging widgets, define logic with a visual action editor, and connect to backends such as Firebase, Supabase, or any API. Because it generates Flutter code, apps run natively on iOS and Android and also on the web, and you can export the code to continue development in a standard IDE, which avoids the lock-in of many no-code tools.

item.title: Fly.io
item.description:
Fly.io lets developers deploy applications near their users. You package an app, often as a Docker container, and Fly runs it in lightweight virtual machines called Machines in many cities, which reduces latency compared with a single centralized region. A command-line tool handles deployment, scaling, and configuration, so a small team can get a global application running without managing servers.

The platform has features useful for modern applications. Machines can start quickly and stop when idle, which suits workloads that spike, private networking links services securely, and volumes provide persistent storage. Managed Postgres and other data services are available, and GPU instances support AI workloads. It’s popular with developers using frameworks such as Rails, Phoenix, Django, and Laravel.

item.title: Forethought AI
item.description: Forethought applies AI to the work that fills support queues. It reads incoming tickets and classifies them by topic and urgency, routes them to the right team, and drafts answers for human agents using the company’s knowledge base and past tickets. For common questions, its AI agents answer directly in chat and email and take simple actions such as checking an order status, handing off to a person when they cannot resolve the issue.

item.title: Formula Bot
item.description:
Formula Bot is aimed at spreadsheet users who know what they want but not the syntax. You describe the calculation, such as finding the average of a column when another column equals a value, and it produces the formula with an explanation. It can also explain a formula you paste in and fix errors, which helps when you inherit a workbook full of nested functions.

The tool extends beyond formulas. It can write scripts, SQL queries, and regular expressions from descriptions, convert between formula dialects, and answer questions about data you upload by building charts and summaries. A chat-style data analysis feature lets users ask questions of a spreadsheet and receive results, aimed at people who don’t write formulas at all.

item.title: Forta
item.description:
Forta provides security monitoring for blockchain applications. Independent developers write detection bots that scan transactions and state changes across networks, looking for patterns that signal attacks, such as sudden fund movements or unusual contract calls. Bots publish alerts to the network, which protocols and users can subscribe to.

Machine learning models are used for some detections, such as spotting scams or anomalies. Protocols use Forta alerts to trigger their own responses, such as pausing contracts. A marketplace of bots covers many threat types and chains, and its token supports staking and rewards for bot operators.

item.title: Foursquare
item.description:
Foursquare began as an app for checking in at places and discovering venues, but its main business today is location data. The company maintains a large database of points of interest, including businesses, landmarks, and venues, with details like categories, hours, and popularity. Developers use its Places API to add search, recommendations, and place information to maps and apps, and brands use its data to understand where people go.

Beyond place data, Foursquare provides tools for analyzing movement and location behavior. Panels of opted-in users allow measurement of foot traffic to stores, audience analysis, and attribution for advertising, and mapping and geospatial products let companies visualize and process location data at scale. Machine learning keeps place information up to date and helps match records from different sources.

item.title: Framer
item.description:
Framer started as a prototyping tool and became a full website builder. Designers lay out pages on a canvas much like they do in Figma, set up responsive behavior, add animations and interactions, and publish to a fast hosted site with a custom domain. Because it gives designers precise control over visuals and motion, it’s popular for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites.

A CMS manages blog posts and other structured content, and features for SEO, localization, and analytics support production sites. AI tools generate a first draft of a site from a description, create wireframes, and write copy, which speeds up the start of a project. Components and code overrides allow customization when needed, and a marketplace of templates and plugins helps.

item.title: Frase
item.description:
Frase helps content teams plan and write articles that can rank. Enter a keyword, and Frase analyzes the top search results to show the topics, questions, and headings they cover and the terms they use, then creates a brief that guides a writer. As you draft, a score shows how well your article covers the topic compared with competitors, and suggestions help fill gaps.

AI features support writing and optimization. Frase can generate outlines and drafts, answer questions drawn from search data, and update existing articles to improve their performance. Newer tools track visibility in AI-generated answers from assistants and search engines, reflecting the shift in how people find information, and an agent can handle parts of the content workflow. Integrations with Google Search Console and publishing tools connect data to action.

item.title: Freepik AI
item.description: Freepik began as a stock site for vectors, photos, and icons, and many designers already knew it. It has added a full AI suite on top. The image generator creates pictures from text prompts, and tools for editing, upscaling, retouching, and expanding images let users refine them. Video generation and animation features turn stills or prompts into short clips, and a workspace organizes projects and lets you mix different tools.

item.title: Freshdesk
item.description: Freshdesk gives support teams a single place to handle customer requests. Messages from email, a web form, live chat, phone, and channels like WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram land in a shared inbox as tickets that can be assigned, tagged, prioritized, and tracked against service-level targets. A knowledge base lets customers find answers on their own, and a customer portal shows the status of their requests. It is used by companies from small startups to large support organizations.

item.title: Gamma
item.description:
Gamma reimagined the presentation. Instead of slides built from a blank template, you describe what you want, such as a pitch for a new product or a lesson on photosynthesis, and Gamma generates a complete, designed deck with text, layouts, and images. The format uses flexible cards that expand and collapse, so presentations can feel more like interactive documents, and it also produces documents and one-page websites.

Editing is conversational and visual. You can ask the AI to rewrite a section, change the style, add images, or restructure, or edit manually with simple controls. Themes keep designs consistent, brand settings apply company fonts and colors, and sharing by link includes analytics on who viewed it. Decks can be exported to PowerPoint or PDF, and it integrates with other tools.

item.title: Gemini
item.description: Gemini is Google’s family of AI models and the assistant built on top of them. You can use it in the standalone Gemini app and website, but it also shows up inside the products many people already use: it can help draft emails in Gmail, rewrite text in Docs, summarize files in Drive, and answer questions on Android phones. If most of your work and personal life already runs on a Google account, that integration is the main reason to choose Gemini over another assistant.

item.title: Gemini Advanced
item.description:
Gemini Advanced was Google’s answer to ChatGPT Plus. When Google rebranded Bard as Gemini, it introduced Advanced as a subscription, sold through Google One, that gave access to its strongest model, longer conversations, and features like file uploads and integration with Gmail and Docs. It also bundled extra Google One storage, which made it attractive to people already paying for cloud storage.

Google later reorganized the plans. Gemini Advanced’s features moved into Google AI Pro, and a higher tier called Google AI Ultra provides the most advanced models, agent features, and generous limits for heavy users. The plans include perks such as video generation, deeper research tools, and integrations with Workspace apps, and the exact lineup changes with each product update.

item.title: Gemini in Workspace
item.description:
Gemini in Workspace brings Google’s models into the apps people use at work. In Gmail, it drafts replies and summarizes long threads. In Docs, it writes, rewrites, and proofreads, and can pull in information from files and email. In Sheets, it helps create formulas, tables, and analysis. In Slides, it generates slides and images, and in Meet it takes notes and summarizes.

A side panel gives a chat assistant that can search across a user’s Drive, Gmail, and Calendar, and answer questions using that content. Organizations can control access, and Google states that business data is not used to train models without permission. Newer features include agents and tools such as NotebookLM for deeper source work.

item.title: Gen-2
item.description:
Runway builds generative video tools for filmmakers, designers, and creators. Gen-3 Alpha was a major step in its line, generating short clips from a text prompt or an image with better detail, motion, and consistency than earlier versions. It supported controls for camera movement and style.

Runway’s platform around its models includes editing tools, motion brush features, and ways to extend or modify clips. Its research focuses on world models and video generation for creative work, and the company works with studios and artists. The newer models in the line have largely taken the place of Gen-3.

item.title: Generated Photos
item.description:
Generated Photos solves a licensing problem: real people’s faces carry privacy and consent obligations, and stock photos can be expensive or restrictive. Its library holds images of faces created by generative models, which depict nobody in particular. Designers use them for website and app mockups, marketers for illustrations, and developers for placeholder avatars in user interfaces.

Several tools extend the library. A face generator lets you pick attributes such as age, gender, ethnicity, hair, and emotion and create new faces, and a photo anonymizer replaces a real face in a picture with a synthetic one. Datasets of synthetic faces serve machine learning teams who need varied images without privacy concerns, and an API provides access for automated use. Full-body and other synthetic image options have been added.

item.title: GetIMG.ai
item.description: getimg.ai provides a web workspace for creating and editing images with AI. You can generate pictures from a prompt using a choice of models, including Stable Diffusion variants and other leading generators, then refine them. Tools for inpainting let you replace part of an image, outpainting extends it past its borders, and an infinite canvas allows you to compose scenes from several generations. Upscaling, background removal, and face tools help finish the result.

item.title: GitHub Copilot
item.description: GitHub Copilot is the AI coding tool with the largest user base, and it is built into the place where most code already lives. It started as inline autocomplete, finishing lines and functions based on the file you were in, and it still does that in VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, and Xcode. A chat panel explains code, writes tests, fixes errors, and answers questions about your project without leaving the editor.

item.title: GitHub Copilot Workspace
item.description: Copilot Workspace was GitHub Next’s attempt to rethink how AI fits into the work of fixing an issue. Starting from a GitHub issue or a prompt, it first wrote a specification of the current and desired behavior, then a plan listing the files to change, and finally the code. At each stage, you could edit the text, so you steered the work in plain English before any code appeared. The finished changes could be opened as a pull request or run in a cloud environment.

item.title: GitLens AI
item.description:
GitLens enriches VS Code with Git history. It shows inline blame annotations that say who last changed a line, when, and in which commit, and lets you browse the history of a file, line, or branch without leaving the editor. Features include a commit graph, comparisons across branches, and a Launchpad that gathers pull requests and issues. It’s one of the most downloaded extensions for VS Code.

AI features help with common Git chores. GitLens can write commit messages from staged changes, summarize what a commit or branch changed in plain language, and help draft pull request descriptions, saving time on documentation. It supports several AI providers and models, with options for how data is sent.

item.title: Gladly
item.description:
Gladly organizes support around the customer, not the ticket. Instead of separate cases for each channel, all interactions with a person appear in a single timeline, so an agent sees the entire history when a customer reaches out. That makes support feel more personal and reduces repeating information.

Sidekick is the AI part. It answers common questions, completes tasks like order lookups, and hands off to a human with context when needed. Assistive features summarize history and suggest replies. Gladly is used by consumer brands that care about the quality of service.

item.title: Glassdoor
item.description:
Glassdoor made workplace information public. Employees write anonymous reviews of their employers, covering culture, management, pay, and benefits, and share salary data and the questions they were asked in interviews. Job seekers use it to research a company before applying or accepting an offer, and to check whether an offer is in line with what others earn in similar roles.

The site also runs a job board and tools for employers. Companies can respond to reviews, post jobs, and promote their employer brand, while job seekers can search listings, set alerts, and apply. AI features appear in job recommendations and in summaries of reviews and salary information. Many of the platform’s operations have been merged with Indeed, its sister site, and Glassdoor is now legally part of Indeed, though the brand and reviews continue.

item.title: Glean
item.description:
Glean addresses the problem that company knowledge lives in dozens of separate tools. It connects to those systems through hundreds of connectors, builds an index of documents, messages, tickets, and other content, and lets employees search across everything from one box. Crucially, it mirrors the permissions of the source systems, so a person only sees results they would already have access to.

On top of search, Glean provides an AI assistant that answers questions in natural language using company information, with citations to the underlying sources. Employees ask things like how a process works, what was decided in a project, or what the latest customer feedback says, and receive a synthesized answer. Glean Agents let teams build automations and agents that take actions in connected apps, and a builder allows non-engineers to create them. Companies can choose among language models from several providers.

item.title: Glide
item.description:
Glide lets people build working apps from a spreadsheet. You connect a sheet or a table, and Glide generates an interface with lists, detail pages, forms, and actions, which you can customize with a visual editor.
