Instead of matching known threats, it learns the usual patterns of each organization, such as which devices talk to which systems and how people normally log in, and then notices when something deviates. This lets it detect novel attacks and insider threats that do not match a known signature. The learning happens inside the customer’s environment, and Darktrace says it does not need to share data with a central model to do it.

item.title: Diffbot
item.description:
Diffbot uses computer vision and natural language processing to read web pages the way a person would. Instead of writing a scraper for each site, developers send a URL to its APIs and receive structured data about articles, products, or people, regardless of page layout.

The company also built a large knowledge graph, a database of entities such as organizations, people, and products, with relationships collected from across the web. Customers query it to enrich records, monitor news, find companies matching criteria, or give language models grounded facts. Its extraction tools support crawling at scale.

item.title: Docsumo
item.description:
Docsumo turns documents into structured data. A company uploads or emails PDFs and scans such as invoices, receipts, bank statements, and forms, and the platform reads fields and tables, checks them against rules, and sends clean data to accounting, lending, or ERP systems. This replaces manual entry.

A review interface lets staff correct uncertain fields, and corrections improve accuracy over time. Pre-trained models cover common documents, while custom models handle company-specific layouts. Workflows include validation rules, approvals, and integrations through APIs. Lenders and finance teams are major users.

item.title: Document360
item.description:
Document360 helps companies maintain help centers and internal documentation. Writers use an editor with categories, versioning, and review workflows, then publish to a branded site that customers or employees can search. Analytics show what people look for and which articles fall short.

AI makes content easier to find and keep up to date. Semantic search finds answers by meaning, a chatbot answers questions from the documentation, and suggestions point out gaps and outdated articles. Writers can also use AI to draft and improve content. Integrations connect with helpdesk and chat tools.

item.title: Dust
item.description:
Dust helps companies deploy AI assistants on their own information. Administrators connect sources such as Notion, Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, and Confluence, and create assistants for functions like support, sales, or engineering. Each assistant has instructions and access to selected data, so answers are grounded in the company’s content.

Employees use assistants in a chat interface or inside Slack, and assistants can take actions through connected tools. Teams share assistants they build, so a good one becomes common property. The platform works with models from several providers, and focuses on security and permissions.

item.title: DVC
item.description:
DVC solves a problem Git was not designed for: large data files. Data scientists track datasets and model files with DVC, which stores small pointer files in Git and keeps the actual data in cloud or local storage such as S3 or Google Cloud Storage. Checking out an old commit retrieves the matching data.

It also supports reproducible pipelines. Users define stages that take data and code as inputs and produce outputs, and DVC reruns only what changed. Experiments can be tracked and compared, and metrics and plots are stored with the repository. The project is now maintained under lakeFS.

item.title: edX
item.description:
edX was founded by Harvard and MIT as a nonprofit to put university courses online. Learners can audit many courses for free or pay for verified certificates, and the catalog includes professional certificates, bootcamps, and online degree programs from partner universities and companies.

The platform later became part of 2U, a company that builds online programs with universities. edX.org remains a major destination for learners seeking credentials, and offers courses in computer science, data, business, and many other fields. Business offerings train employees. The open-source Open edX software that powers many other learning sites is separate from edX.org.

item.title: Evidently AI
item.description:
Evidently helps teams know whether their models are working. The open-source library computes metrics and produces interactive reports on data drift, data quality, model accuracy, and, for language model applications, aspects such as relevance and safety. It can run in notebooks, in pipelines, or as a monitoring service.

For LLM work, Evidently supports evaluations with test sets, automated judges, and tracing, so teams can compare prompt versions and catch regressions. A hosted platform adds dashboards, alerting, and collaboration, and the project has a large community and educational material on ML observability.

item.title: Evisort
item.description:
Evisort uses AI to understand contracts. It ingests agreements, identifies clauses and key terms such as renewal dates, payment terms, and liability limits, and stores them as structured data. Teams can search across thousands of contracts, instead of hunting through PDFs.

It supports the contract lifecycle: drafting from templates, negotiating, tracking obligations, and getting alerts before renewals. Reports show risk and spend across the portfolio. Generative AI helps review contracts against playbooks and suggests changes.

item.title: Factory AI
item.description:
Factory sells AI agents for engineering teams. Droids take tasks from tickets or chat, explore a codebase, make changes, run tests, and open pull requests for review. Specialized droids handle different jobs, such as code review, incident response, or migrations.

The product works through a command line tool, IDE integrations, and a web interface, and connects to GitHub, Jira, Slack, and other tools so agents fit into existing workflows. Enterprise features address security, permissions, and model choice, with support for several model providers.

item.title: Fal.ai
item.description:
fal.ai gives developers a fast way to use generative media models without managing GPUs. A team calls an API for models that produce images, video, audio, and 3D assets, and fal handles the infrastructure, scaling, and optimization. Its speed is the main pitch, which matters for apps where users wait on each generation.

The catalog includes popular open models and models from partners, and the platform is used by consumer apps, design tools, and companies that add generation features to their products. Developers can also deploy their own models and fine-tunes on its serverless compute, and use dedicated GPUs for steady workloads.

item.title: Fantastical
item.description:
Fantastical is known for natural language entry. A user types a phrase such as lunch with Sam next Tuesday at noon, and the app creates the event with the right time, place, and attendees. It shows calendars from many accounts in one view, including Google, iCloud, and Exchange, along with tasks and reminders.

Scheduling features help with coordination. Users can share availability and let others book time, propose several slots to a group, and attach video conference details automatically. Newer AI features help with preparation for meetings and smart suggestions, and the app integrates with other tools through its calendar sets and openings.

item.title: Fish Audio
item.description:
Fish Audio generates synthetic speech with an emphasis on voice variety. Users type text, choose a voice, and get audio. A cloning feature creates a voice from a short sample, and a public library offers voices shared by other users, including character and celebrity-style options.

Creators use it for narration, videos, games, and podcasts, and developers integrate it through an API for apps and agents. The company has released open models for speech synthesis, which has helped it build a community of users and researchers.

item.title: Flatiron Health
item.description:
Flatiron Health works in cancer care. Its electronic health record, OncoEMR, is used by many community oncology practices, and the data from those practices, once de-identified and curated, form a large real-world dataset. Researchers use it to study how treatments work outside clinical trials.

The company uses machine learning and human abstraction to turn unstructured notes into research-ready data. Biopharma companies use these datasets to understand patient populations, design trials, and support regulatory submissions. Products for clinics include tools for clinical workflows, billing, and trial matching.

item.title: Folk
item.description:
Folk is a relationship manager for people who find traditional CRMs heavy. Users import contacts from email, LinkedIn, and spreadsheets, organize them into groups, and track conversations and deals in a clean interface. It suits agencies, recruiters, investors, and founders who manage many relationships.

AI and automation reduce the manual work. Enrichment fills in details like company and role, a browser extension saves profiles from LinkedIn, and sequences send personalized emails at scale. AI helps write messages and summarize history, and reminders prompt follow-ups so nobody falls through the cracks.

item.title: Freshsales
item.description:
Freshsales is a sales CRM that keeps lead and deal information in one view. Teams track contacts, run pipelines, and log calls and emails, with a built-in phone and chat so reps can contact prospects without switching tools. Automation moves leads through stages and assigns tasks.

Freddy AI assists with prioritization. It scores leads by likelihood to convert, predicts which deals will close, and suggests next best actions, while generative features draft emails and summarize conversations. Analytics show pipeline health, and integrations connect with Freshdesk, marketing tools, and common business apps.

item.title: Front
item.description:
Front treats shared inboxes like collaborative workspaces. Support, sales, and account teams manage messages from several channels in one place, assign conversations, leave internal comments, and see who is handling what. The interface resembles email, so adoption is easy.

Automation and AI reduce manual work. Rules route messages, tag them, and set priorities, while AI summarizes long threads, suggests replies, and answers common questions. Analytics show response times and workloads, and integrations with CRMs and helpdesk tools provide context.

item.title: Gem
item.description:
Gem helps recruiting teams build pipelines. Recruiters search for candidates across LinkedIn and other sources, add them to talent pools, and send sequences of personalized outreach. A candidate CRM tracks every interaction, so when a role opens, the team can reach people they have already engaged.

Analytics show how sourcing channels perform, how long hiring takes, and where candidates drop out. AI features help with search, writing outreach, and identifying candidates who may be open to new roles. An applicant tracking system component extends the suite for teams that want everything in one place.

item.title: Ghost
item.description:
Ghost is a publishing tool focused on independent media. It provides a clean editor, a website with themes, email newsletters, and a membership system that lets readers subscribe for free or pay. Because it is open source, publishers can host it themselves or use Ghost’s managed service.

Business features are built in. Payments run through Stripe, so publishers keep most of the revenue, and analytics show how posts convert readers into members. The platform supports multiple tiers, comments, and integrations with other tools. A nonprofit organization develops it, which differs from venture-backed rivals.

item.title: Giskard
item.description:
Giskard focuses on quality and safety testing for AI. A team connects a model or an application, and the tool generates test cases and probes to find weaknesses. It checks for factual errors, harmful outputs, prompt injection, sensitive data exposure, and unfair behavior across groups.

Findings become a test suite that can run continuously, for example in a CI pipeline, so regressions are caught before release. For language model applications, Giskard supports retrieval-augmented systems and offers a red-teaming approach with automated attacks. A hub provides collaboration and reports for risk and compliance teams.

item.title: Gladia
item.description:
Gladia provides speech-to-text as a service for developers. Companies send audio from calls, meetings, or videos and receive transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and optional translation. It handles dozens of languages and can detect which one is being spoken.

Real-time transcription suits live captioning and voice agents, while batch processing handles recordings at scale. Extra features include summaries, sentiment, and named entity detection. The API is aimed at products built on audio, such as meeting assistants, call analytics, and media tools.

item.title: Guru
item.description:
Guru stores verified knowledge in cards that teams can find where they work. A browser extension and Slack integration surface relevant answers without leaving the page, and experts verify cards on a schedule so that the information stays trustworthy. The idea is a single source of truth for sales, support, and internal teams.

AI search connects to the company’s other sources, such as documents, chat, and ticketing systems, and answers questions in natural language with citations. Analytics show what people search for and which content is stale. Admins control who can see what, and the AI respects those permissions.

item.title: Hedra
item.description:
Hedra animates faces. A user supplies a still image, which can be a photo, illustration, or generated character, and an audio track or script, and Hedra produces a video of the character speaking with matching lip movement and expression. The results are known for emotive performances.

Uses include short films, explainer videos, social content with characters, and marketing. Text to speech and voice options make it possible to start from only a script, and longer and higher resolution outputs are available on paid plans. The platform has expanded into broader video generation features.

item.title: Helicone
item.description:
Helicone gives teams visibility into their language model usage. A developer changes the base URL of their API calls to route through Helicone, and each request is logged with its prompt, response, latency, cost, and user. Dashboards show spend by model, user, or feature, and flag errors.

Additional tools help manage production use. Caching saves cost on repeated requests, rate limits protect budgets, and prompt management lets teams version and test prompts. Sessions group multi-step agent traces, and evaluation features score outputs.

item.title: Humanloop
item.description:
Humanloop helped teams build reliable applications on language models. Developers managed and versioned prompts, ran automated and human evaluations, and monitored behavior in production. It was used by enterprises that needed to test changes before shipping and keep a record of how prompts evolved.

Anthropic hired the company’s co-founders and most of its team, without acquiring the product or its intellectual property. The standalone service was wound down shortly afterward, and customers were given guidance for migrating to other tools.

item.title: HyperScience
item.description:
HyperScience automates paperwork-heavy processes. Organizations in insurance, banking, and government feed forms, letters, and claims into the platform, which classifies each document, extracts fields, and passes clean data to downstream systems. Handwriting recognition covers documents that older tools struggled with.

A human-in-the-loop design handles low-confidence results: reviewers check flagged fields, and their corrections improve the models. The platform has added large language model features for understanding unstructured text and answering questions about documents, and it supports on-premises and private cloud deployment for sensitive data.

item.title: HyperWrite
item.description:
HyperWrite started as a writing tool that predicted and completed text as you typed. It grew into a suite that includes a document editor, a browser extension that works across websites, and tools for rewriting, summarizing, and researching. Users can generate text from prompts and refine it in place.

The company has focused on agents. An assistant can navigate web pages, fill in forms, and complete multi-step tasks in the browser on a user’s behalf, which fits its idea of a personal AI assistant. It supports multiple underlying models.

item.title: Iconosquare
item.description:
Iconosquare started as an Instagram analytics tool and expanded to other networks. Social teams connect accounts and see how posts perform, when audiences are active, and how growth compares with competitors. Reports can be exported for clients, which makes it popular with agencies.

Scheduling and planning tools let teams build a content calendar and publish across networks. AI features suggest captions and hashtags, and a listening module monitors mentions and comments. The focus is on analysis that guides what to post, more than on broad community management.

item.title: Inngest
item.description:
Inngest lets developers define workflows in code that survive failures. A function is broken into steps, and Inngest stores the result of each step, retries failures, and resumes where it left off. This suits tasks like processing orders, sending sequences of emails, and running AI agent chains that take a long time.

It is designed for serverless platforms such as Vercel and AWS Lambda, where long-running processes are awkward. Features include event triggers, scheduled runs, rate limiting, concurrency control, and a dashboard to inspect runs and replay failures. It supports TypeScript, Python, and Go.

item.title: Insider
item.description:
Insider helps brands treat each visitor differently. It collects behavior data across channels, builds unified profiles, and uses them to personalize websites, app experiences, and messages. A marketer can design a journey that reaches a customer by email, then push, then SMS depending on what they do.

The AI layer predicts what people are likely to buy or whether they may churn, recommends products, and optimizes timing and content. The platform also includes tools for search, recommendations, and conversational commerce. It is used heavily by retailers and consumer brands in many regions.

item.title: Instabase
item.description:
Instabase focuses on complex documents that older template-based tools could not handle. Mortgage packages, insurance claims, and financial statements arrive in many formats, and Instabase uses AI models to classify them, extract data, and validate it against rules. Results flow into systems such as loan origination and claims platforms.

Its platform provides tools for building document workflows with a mix of models and human review, and newer products use language models for understanding and answering questions about documents. Customers can deploy it in the cloud or in their own environment, which matters for regulated data.

item.title: Iterable
item.description:
Iterable lets marketers build cross-channel journeys. They segment customers by behavior, design workflows in a visual canvas, and send messages triggered by actions, such as signing up, abandoning a cart, or reaching a milestone. Data from websites, apps, and warehouses feeds the profile used for personalization.

AI assists in several areas: optimizing the time a message is sent for each person, predicting engagement, recommending content, and helping generate copy. Experimentation tools test variants, and analytics tie campaigns to outcomes. Integration with data warehouses supports teams that centralize customer data.

item.title: Jammable
item.description:
Jammable, formerly Voicify, lets people hear songs sung in a different voice. A user chooses a voice model from a library, uploads a vocal or song, and the system converts it so it sounds like the chosen voice. Fans and creators use it for parodies, mashups, and experiments.

The technology raises serious legal and ethical issues. Voices of real artists are protected in many places, and music labels and artists have objected to unauthorized voice clones. Sharing such covers can violate copyright and rights of publicity, and platforms may remove them. Use voices you have permission to use, and avoid presenting synthetic songs as the real artist.

item.title: Jiminny
item.description:
Jiminny captures conversations between sales teams and customers. It records calls and meetings, creates transcripts, and uses AI to summarize them, extract action items, and detect topics, objections, and talk ratios. Managers use this to coach reps with specific examples.

Deal insights help forecast. The platform flags risks such as lack of next steps or missing stakeholders, and keeps the CRM updated with notes and fields without manual entry. Search across calls lets teams find how customers talk about competitors or pricing.

item.title: Jina AI
item.description:
Jina AI focuses on the retrieval side of AI applications. Its embedding models turn text and images into vectors for search in many languages, rerankers sort results by relevance, and a reader API converts a web page into clean text that language models can use. Search and deep research endpoints build on these.

Many developers used Jina’s open models from Hugging Face and its free-to-start APIs when building retrieval-augmented generation. The company also open-sourced framework projects for building multimodal systems in its early years.

item.title: Jira
item.description:
Jira tracks work through issues in boards, backlogs, and timelines. Software teams use it for sprints, bug tracking, and roadmaps, and many other teams use it for requests and projects. Workflows are customizable, and it integrates with code hosts, chat tools, and the rest of Atlassian’s products.

Atlassian has added AI across Jira. It summarizes long ticket discussions, drafts descriptions and subtasks, and turns natural language into search queries. Rovo agents can take on work such as triaging issues or answering questions across connected tools, and the AI draws on a team’s own data.

item.title: Kaiber
item.description:
Kaiber is known for stylized, artistic video. A user supplies a prompt, an image, or a video clip, chooses a style, and the platform generates moving footage in that look. Audio reactivity lets visuals respond to a music track, which made it a favorite for music videos and live visuals.

The platform has grown into a broader creative studio with a canvas for combining generated images and video and with access to several underlying models. Artists use it to experiment with motion and aesthetics rather than realistic footage, and it has been featured in music video projects.

item.title: Kinaxis
item.description:
Kinaxis helps large manufacturers and retailers plan and respond. Its platform brings demand, supply, inventory, and capacity into one model that updates together, rather than in separate steps, so planners can test the effect of a disruption or a decision in minutes.

Planners run what-if scenarios, see the impact on service and cost, and collaborate across functions. Machine learning improves demand sensing and supply risk detection, and newer AI agents help summarize issues and recommend actions. Customers include companies in high tech, life sciences, automotive, and consumer goods.

item.title: Kits AI
item.description:
Kits AI targets music creators. A producer can record a vocal and convert it into another singer’s voice from a library, create a model of their own voice for consistent takes, or separate a song into vocals and instruments to remix. A text to speech option and tools for vocal cleanup are included.

Its distinguishing approach is licensing. Kits offers voices from artists who have agreed to participate and be paid, which contrasts with unauthorized voice clones that raise copyright and rights-of-publicity problems. Users still need to follow license terms for how converted vocals are released.

item.title: Kixie
item.description:
Kixie speeds up phone outreach. A power dialer calls through a list automatically, local presence shows numbers with the prospect’s area code to improve answer rates, and voicemail drop leaves a prerecorded message with one click. Calls and texts sync with CRMs such as HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive.

Automation sends text messages and follow-ups triggered by call outcomes, and a coaching feature lets managers listen in. AI transcribes calls, summarizes them, and gives feedback on conversations. Analytics track activity, connect rates, and results by rep.

item.title: Klap
item.description:
Klap helps creators and marketers turn long videos into shorts. A user uploads a video or pastes a link, and the tool picks promising segments, crops them to vertical format while tracking the speaker, and adds captions. A score estimates how likely each clip is to perform.

The clips can be edited to adjust timing, captions, and layout, and published or exported. Podcasters, coaches, webinar hosts, and YouTubers use it to get more mileage from content they already have. Language support lets clips be captioned or dubbed for other audiences.

item.title: Klevu
item.description:
Klevu improves how online shoppers find products. Instead of matching keywords exactly, its search engine uses natural language processing to interpret queries, handle synonyms and misspellings, and rank results based on relevance and merchandising goals. It works with platforms such as Shopify, Magento, and BigCommerce.

The product also includes category browsing, recommendations, and analytics on what shoppers search for and fail to find. Merchandisers can adjust results with rules, and AI personalization adapts to a shopper’s behavior. A chat-style assistant answers product questions.

item.title: Lakera
item.description:
Lakera defends applications built on language models. Its Guard product sits between users and a model, scanning prompts for attempts to override instructions, extract secrets, or inject malicious content, and checking outputs for leaks and harmful material. Developers add it with an API call.

The company grew out of research on adversarial attacks and became known for Gandalf, a public game where players try to trick a model into revealing a password, which generated a large dataset of attacks. Red teaming tools test applications before launch.

item.title: LanceDB
item.description:
LanceDB is a database for AI data. It stores vectors alongside the original data, such as text, images, and video references, and supports similarity search, filtering, and full-text search. Because it is embedded, it runs inside an application with no server, similar to how SQLite works for relational data.

The Lance format makes it efficient for large datasets: it keeps data on disk, supports versioning, and allows fast random access, so it can handle collections that do not fit in memory. A cloud and enterprise offering adds scalability and managed service. It is used for retrieval in AI applications and for managing training data.

item.title: Langfuse
item.description:
Langfuse gives developers visibility into LLM applications. By adding its SDK or an integration, each request is traced with its prompts, model responses, tool calls, latency, and cost, including nested steps in agent workflows. Engineers inspect failures in a web interface and see usage across users and sessions.

Beyond observability, it supports quality work. Prompt management lets teams version and deploy prompts without code changes, evaluation features score outputs through LLM judges, user feedback, or custom checks, and datasets let teams run experiments before release. The product can be self-hosted, which suits privacy-sensitive teams.

item.title: LangSmith
item.description:
LangSmith helps teams understand and improve AI applications. Developers send traces from their applications, and LangSmith shows each step: prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls, and model outputs, with timing and cost. This makes it possible to find where an agent went wrong.

Evaluation is the second pillar. Teams build datasets from real traffic, run experiments across prompt or model versions, and score results with automated evaluators or human review. Monitoring dashboards and alerts track quality in production, and a deployment product hosts agents built with LangGraph.

item.title: Latitude
item.description:
Latitude makes interactive fiction with AI. Its best-known product, AI Dungeon, lets players describe any action in natural language, and an AI game master responds with the next part of the story. The result is open-ended storytelling that can go in any direction, from fantasy quests to comedy and mystery.

The studio has experimented with other AI-driven games and with platforms for creators who want to build their own AI-powered worlds. It uses a mix of language models, including models it trains and fine-tunes, and offers different tiers of models to subscribers.

item.title: Latte Social
item.description:
Latte Social covers the basics of content planning. Users connect accounts, ask the AI for post ideas and captions tuned to a brand’s voice, schedule content on a calendar, and publish to several networks. The tool aims to keep a steady posting schedule without constant effort.

For small teams and individual creators, that combination of drafting and scheduling reduces time spent on routine social tasks. AI-generated posts are a starting point and tend to be generic without personal details and specific examples.

item.title: Lever
item.description:
Lever pairs two things that recruiting teams often keep separate: an applicant tracking system for people who apply, and a relationship manager for people you want to attract. In one place, recruiters post jobs, move candidates through stages, schedule interviews, collect feedback, and build talent pools for roles that open later. The pipeline view is visual and quick to scan, which suits teams that hire continuously.

Sourcing and nurture are a focus. Lever can run email sequences to passive candidates, track responses, and bring prospects into the same pipeline as applicants. Interview scheduling is automated so recruiters spend less time on calendars, and scorecards keep feedback structured. Reporting covers the funnel, diversity data, and time to hire. Integrations link it to job boards, HR systems, and assessment tools.

item.title: Lexica
item.description:
Lexica began as a searchable archive of AI-generated images with the prompts that created them. Browsing the archive helped people learn how wording affects results, and copy ideas for their own generations. That made it a popular learning resource in the early days of image generators.

The platform added its own image generation models and an editor, so users can create images, refine them, and organize collections. It offers different model options and tools for art, product shots, and concepts. The community library remains a source of inspiration.

item.title: Lindy AI
item.description:
Lindy AI is the product behind agents called Lindies. A user assembles an agent from triggers, actions, and instructions, linking it to services such as Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, and CRMs. The agent can then run tasks like replying to routine messages, scheduling meetings, and logging notes.

Typical deployments include an executive assistant that manages an inbox and calendar, a sales assistant that researches leads and updates records, and a support helper that answers common questions. Agents can ask for approval before sensitive actions, which keeps a person in the loop.

item.title: LiteLLM
item.description:
LiteLLM solves the problem of integrating many model providers. Developers write code once against the OpenAI format, and LiteLLM translates the call to the provider they choose. Switching models then means changing a name, not rewriting code.

The proxy server adds features for teams: a gateway with virtual keys, budgets and rate limits per team, logging, load balancing across deployments, and automatic fallback when a provider fails. Platform teams use it to give internal users a controlled path to models and to track costs.

item.title: Litera
item.description:
Litera is known for products lawyers use daily. Its comparison software shows exactly what changed between document versions, a core need in contract negotiation, and drafting tools check formatting, cross-references, and defined terms. Other products handle transaction management and closing checklists.

Newer AI features help review documents, summarize them, and spot inconsistencies or risk. The company has combined many acquired products into a suite for law firms and corporate legal departments, and it integrates with Microsoft Word and document management systems.

item.title: Loomly
item.description:
Loomly supports the planning side of social media. Teams build a content calendar, get post ideas from trends and prompts, draft posts with images and links, and route them through an approval workflow before publishing. A brand asset library keeps logos and images handy.

The platform previews how a post will look on each network and schedules publishing. Analytics show performance, and ad management features support boosted posts. AI assists with captions and ideas.

item.title: Lummi
item.description:
Lummi collects AI-generated pictures in a searchable library, organized by category and style. Users browse or search for backgrounds, textures, scenes, and illustrations, then download them for use in websites, presentations, and campaigns. The pitch is variety and a modern look compared with familiar stock photography.

The platform includes generation tools that let users create images from prompts and adjust them, along with options for editing. It is popular with designers who want unusual or abstract visuals and do not want to prompt from scratch.

item.title: Lyra Health
item.description:
Lyra provides employer-sponsored mental health care. Employees take an assessment and are matched with a provider from Lyra’s network of clinicians, with options for therapy, coaching, medication management, and digital programs. Employers pay for the benefit, so employees may have little or no out-of-pocket cost for a set number of sessions.

The company says it focuses on quality and outcomes by vetting providers and measuring progress. AI supports the matching process, helps clinicians with documentation, and powers a conversational tool offering support between sessions, while keeping clinicians involved in care.

item.title: Madgicx
item.description:
Madgicx is built for performance marketers and e-commerce brands running paid social. It connects to ad accounts and analyzes campaigns, then recommends or applies changes such as shifting budget toward better-performing ad sets, pausing losers, or testing new audiences. Automation rules run these changes continuously.

Creative tools help with the content side. The platform analyzes which creatives perform best and helps generate variations, and reporting dashboards combine data from ads and online stores into one view. Audience tools find lookalike segments and retargeting groups.

item.title: Magnific AI
item.description:
Magnific AI takes a low-resolution image and produces a larger version with added, invented detail. Users control how much creative freedom the AI takes with settings such as creativity and resemblance, and can add a prompt describing what the detail should look like. This makes it different from conventional upscalers.

Artists use it to polish AI-generated images and to turn rough concept art into detailed illustrations. Designers use it to prepare images for large formats. The company was acquired by Freepik, and the technology is available through Magnific’s own site and Freepik’s tools.

item.title: Marqo
item.description:
Marqo handles vector search end to end. A developer sends documents or images to Marqo, and it generates embeddings with a chosen model, stores them, and serves similarity queries, so there is no separate pipeline for embedding and indexing. Queries can combine text and images, which suits product search.

The company has focused on e-commerce relevance, offering models trained for product search and tools to improve ranking with feedback from user behavior. It runs as a self-hosted open-source service or as a managed cloud.

item.title: Mastra
item.description:
Mastra targets JavaScript and TypeScript developers who build AI features. It provides building blocks: agents that call tools, workflows with steps and branching, retrieval over documents, memory, evaluations, and observability. Developers can run it locally with a playground to test and debug.

Its design fits the web stack, with deployment options for serverless platforms and integration with frameworks like Next.js. It works with models from many providers through a common interface and supports the Model Context Protocol. A hosted platform offers deployment and monitoring.

item.title: Matterport
item.description:
Matterport captures spaces in 3D. A camera or a phone scans a property, and the software stitches the data into a navigable model, a virtual tour where viewers can walk through rooms, take measurements, and view floor plans. Real estate agents use it to show listings, and others use it to document sites.

Beyond tours, the platform serves professional needs. Contractors document existing conditions, insurers record property states, and facility managers keep a digital record of buildings. AI helps generate floor plans, label rooms, and create other outputs from scans.

item.title: Mavenoid
item.description:
Mavenoid focuses on products people have trouble setting up or fixing. Instead of a long manual or a phone queue, customers use an interactive guide that asks questions, narrows down the problem, and walks through steps with pictures and videos. If the guide cannot solve it, it hands off to support with the details collected.

Manufacturers build these flows from their manuals and support data, and AI helps generate and maintain content, answer free-text questions, and spot recurring issues. Analytics show where customers get stuck, which feeds back to product teams.

item.title: Mem0
item.description:
Mem0 gives AI applications a long-term memory. Language models forget everything between conversations unless the application supplies context. Mem0 extracts important facts from interactions, stores them, and retrieves the relevant ones when needed, so a chatbot can recall a user’s preferences or past requests.

Developers add it with a few API calls or a library, and it works with common models and frameworks. It supports user, session, and agent level memory, and a hosted platform manages storage and scaling. Use cases include personal assistants, customer support, and tutoring.

item.title: Mercury
item.description: Mercury provides online banking designed for startups. A founder can open a business account in minutes, get checking and savings, send and receive wires and ACH transfers, issue virtual and physical debit and credit cards, and pay bills, all in a clean web and mobile interface. Mercury is a financial technology company, not a bank itself, and works with partner banks to hold deposits and provide FDIC insurance through sweep arrangements.

item.title: Metaflow
item.description:
Metaflow lets data scientists write workflows as plain Python classes. Steps are functions, and the framework tracks code, data, and parameters for each run, so any result can be reproduced. It scales steps out to cloud compute with a decorator, without making the scientist learn infrastructure.

Netflix built it to let data scientists move from a laptop experiment to production on their own. Features include versioned artifacts, scheduling through orchestrators such as Argo Workflows and AWS Step Functions, and a UI for inspecting runs. Outerbounds, a company founded by Metaflow’s creators, offers a managed platform.

item.title: Milvus
item.description:
Milvus is built for scale. It stores high-dimensional vectors, which represent text, images, or other data, and finds the nearest neighbors quickly even among billions of items. It supports different index types, filtering with metadata, and hybrid search that combines vectors and keywords.

The architecture separates storage and compute so it can run across a cluster, and there are lighter modes for development. It is part of the Linux Foundation’s AI & Data group, and Zilliz offers a managed cloud service with additional features.

item.title: Moises
item.description:
Moises helps musicians work with recordings. A user uploads a song, and the app splits it into individual tracks, so a guitarist can mute the guitar and play along, or a singer can remove the lead vocal for practice. Tempo and key changes help with learning difficult parts.

Extra tools include chord detection, a metronome, and a feature to detect beats. Producers use stem separation for remixes and sampling, and teachers use it to demonstrate parts. Mobile and web apps make it easy to practice anywhere.

item.title: Monarch Money
item.description:
Monarch Money brings accounts into one dashboard. Users link banks, cards, loans, and investments, and the app tracks spending, net worth, and recurring bills. Budgets can follow a flexible or category-based model, and goals help save toward targets.

Couples and families can share views and manage budgets together while keeping some accounts private. AI categorizes transactions, spots subscriptions, and gives summaries and insights, and an assistant answers questions about finances. Reports show trends over time.

item.title: Morph Studio
item.description:
Morph Studio lets users create video through prompts and images. It offers a storyboard interface, where a creator plans shots, generates each, and assembles them into a sequence, which suits narrative content more than single clips. Different models and styles are available.

Creators use it for short films, ads, music videos, and social content. The workflow supports iteration: regenerate a shot, adjust the prompt, and compare results. Community features let users share work and learn techniques.

item.title: MultiOn
item.description:
MultiOn was one of the early companies to build browser-using agents. A user gives an instruction in plain language, and the agent navigates sites, clicks, types, and completes the steps, keeping a session going across pages. Developers could call it through an API to build agents of their own.

The company has talked about moving into a new phase, and directories describe a change of name and focus, though accounts differ. That makes it worth checking the official site to see what is currently available before depending on it.

item.title: Musicfy
item.description:
Musicfy offers several music tools in one place. Users can generate a track from a text prompt, convert one instrument or vocal to another voice or sound, separate a song into stems, and create voice covers with AI voices. It is aimed at creators who want to experiment with songs without a studio.

The same tools raise rights questions. Copying a real artist’s voice without permission can violate publicity and copyright rules, and platforms and labels remove such content. Generated music has varying licensing terms, so read them before releasing or monetizing songs.

item.title: Mutiny
item.description:
Mutiny changes what a website says depending on the visitor. If a visitor comes from a target account, an industry, or a campaign, Mutiny swaps in headlines, proof points, and calls to action that fit, using firmographic data and ad information. Marketers set this up in a visual editor without developers.

AI recommends segments and generates alternative copy, then tests variations and reports on conversions. Integrations connect with CRMs, ad platforms, and customer data tools so personalization can follow account-based marketing programs.

item.title: Nabla
item.description:
Nabla works as a scribe in the exam room. During a visit, with consent, it captures the conversation and creates a structured note in the clinician’s preferred format, which they review and copy into the health record. It also drafts letters and patient instructions from the same encounter.

The company began in France and has expanded to the United States and elsewhere, with support for multiple languages and specialties. It emphasizes privacy, including not retaining audio after processing, and integrates with electronic health record systems.

item.title: Nanonets
item.description:
Nanonets turns documents into data. A company sends invoices, purchase orders, receipts, or forms by email or upload, and the platform reads them, extracts fields and line items, and validates them against rules. Approved data flows into accounting or ERP systems.

Pre-trained models cover common documents, and teams can train models for their own layouts with a few samples. Workflows add approval steps, matching against purchase orders, and exception handling. Language models help with messy or varied documents.

item.title: Neon
item.description:
Neon runs PostgreSQL in the cloud with a design that lets databases scale to zero when idle and start quickly when needed. Because storage and compute are separate, it can create copy-on-write branches of a database instantly, which suits testing, previews, and development workflows.

Branching has become useful for AI work, where agents and coding tools create databases on the fly. The pgvector extension supports embeddings and similarity search, so developers can store vectors next to ordinary data. The platform is used with frameworks like Next.js and with serverless hosts.

item.title: Nightfall AI
item.description:
Nightfall protects data in the tools companies use daily. It connects to applications such as Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, and Salesforce, scans content for sensitive items like personal data, payment details, and API keys, and alerts or acts when it finds them. Detection relies on machine learning rather than only pattern matching.

Remediation features can redact, quarantine, or delete exposed data, and notify users with guidance. The company has added protection for AI use, scanning prompts and uploads to chat tools so employees do not paste confidential information into models.

item.title: Nous Research
item.description:
Nous Research started as a group of researchers and hobbyists working in the open. Its Hermes models fine-tune open base models to follow instructions, use tools, and handle roleplay and reasoning, and have been popular among people running models locally. Data, methods, and weights are shared publicly.

The group has also worked on decentralized training, exploring ways to train large models across many machines run by different parties, and on tooling for agents. It operates as a company and offers access to its models through an API and an agent product.

item.title: Octane AI
item.description:
Octane AI lets stores add an interactive quiz to their site. Shoppers answer questions about preferences, and the quiz recommends products and captures their answers and contact details. Because customers volunteer the information, it is called zero-party data, and it supports personalized email and text marketing.

The platform integrates with Shopify and marketing tools such as Klaviyo, so quiz results can feed segments and flows. Brands use it for skincare, supplements, food, and other categories where choosing among many products is hard. Analytics show how quizzes affect conversion.

item.title: Oliv AI
item.description:
Oliv AI assists sellers before, during, and after calls. Before a meeting, it gathers context on the account and contacts and drafts a briefing. During the call, it records and transcribes. Afterward, it writes notes, updates the CRM, and drafts follow-up emails.

For managers, it scores deals against frameworks such as MEDDIC and highlights risks and gaps, which supports coaching and forecasting. The product presents these functions as agents that take over routine sales admin.

item.title: Pallyy
item.description:
Pallyy keeps social management simple and affordable. Users connect accounts, plan posts on a visual calendar, and publish to several networks. A first-comment feature, link-in-bio pages, and a media library support common creator workflows, and a unified inbox collects comments and messages.

Analytics show growth and engagement, and client-friendly reports help agencies prove results. Collaboration tools let clients approve content before it goes live. AI features suggest captions, hashtags, and ideas to speed up planning.

item.title: Paradox
item.description:
Paradox focuses on hiring for roles with many applicants, such as retail, hospitality, and logistics. Olivia chats with candidates by text or on a career site, asks qualifying questions, answers common questions about the job and company, and books interviews directly on managers’ calendars.

That removes much of the scheduling and screening back and forth that slows recruiting. Candidates get fast responses, and recruiters spend time on interviews instead of coordination. The platform includes an applicant tracking tool and onboarding support.

item.title: Paragraph AI
item.description:
Paragraph AI brings AI writing to the smartphone. A user types a few words or dictates an idea, and the app produces a full email, message, or post, which can be adjusted for tone, length, or formality. Rewrite and proofreading tools tidy existing text.

The appeal is convenience for writing on the go, when opening a full desktop assistant is awkward. Typical uses include replying to emails, drafting social captions, and polishing short messages.

item.title: PathAI
item.description:
PathAI works on digital pathology. Pathologists traditionally examine tissue slides under a microscope. With scanned slides, algorithms can highlight regions of interest, count cells, and measure biomarkers, which helps make reads more consistent. PathAI builds these tools and a platform for viewing and managing slides.

The company also supports pharmaceutical research. Its models analyze tissue from clinical trials to measure disease features and treatment responses, and it operates a laboratory service. The goal is to reduce variability and speed drug development.

item.title: Patronus AI
item.description:
Patronus AI helps teams find problems in AI applications. Developers run test sets through their systems, and Patronus scores the outputs with evaluators that check for hallucinations, unsafe content, leaks of sensitive data, and policy violations. Red-teaming tools probe for weaknesses with adversarial inputs.

The company has published benchmarks, including tests for financial question answering, and trained evaluation models such as a judge model for hallucination detection. Monitoring features watch production traffic and alert teams to drops in quality.

item.title: PearAI
item.description:
PearAI is a standalone editor forked from VS Code, with AI features built in. Developers get code completion, a chat panel that understands the project, and inline editing, and can connect their preferred models. Because it is a fork, familiar extensions and settings carry over.

It positions itself as an open alternative to Cursor and Windsurf. The AI layer builds on Continue, an open-source assistant. The project had a licensing controversy early on regarding its use of existing code, which it has since addressed.

item.title: Phenom
item.description:
Phenom helps employers attract and manage talent. Its career sites show candidates jobs and content tailored to their interests, a recruiting CRM nurtures talent pools, and tools handle scheduling, chat, and applications. The same platform supports employees through internal job matching and career paths.

AI infers skills from resumes and profiles to match people with roles, recommend jobs, and surface candidates already in the system. Analytics show the hiring funnel and diversity data. The company sells to large enterprises.

item.title: Pimsleur
item.description:
Pimsleur is an audio-first method developed by linguist Paul Pimsleur. Each short lesson has the learner listen to a conversation, repeat phrases aloud, and answer prompts, with vocabulary reintroduced at expanding intervals so it moves into memory. Lessons are designed for use while commuting or doing chores.

The app offers many languages and adds features such as reading lessons, flashcards, and speech practice. Its approach centers on speaking and listening more than grammar rules or writing.

item.title: PixAI
item.description:
PixAI is built around anime-style generation. Users type prompts, pick models trained for particular looks, and generate images. A feed of community creations offers inspiration, and sharing prompts lets others learn techniques.

Features include image-to-image transformation, model and LoRA libraries, and tools for creating characters consistently. A mobile app and credit system support casual use.

PixAI has a free tier with daily credits and paid plans. Community models can be trained on artwork without artists’ consent, which is controversial, and content rules apply to the platform. Alternatives include Civitai, Leonardo AI, NovelAI, Midjourney with niji, and Tensor.Art. PixAI suits anime fans and illustrators exploring AI art.

item.title: Plandex
item.description:
Plandex works in the terminal and aims at tasks that span many files. It plans a change, builds it up in a sandbox so edits can be reviewed before they touch your project, and supports long context windows to keep track of large repositories. Changes can be rolled back, and different models can be used for different steps.

The team behind it announced that Plandex Cloud would wind down, leaving the self-hosted open-source server and CLI. That means new users need to run it themselves, and development activity has slowed, so check the repository for current maintenance.

item.title: Podcastle
item.description:
Podcastle is a browser-based studio for audio. Users can record remote interviews with separate tracks, edit by working with the transcript, and clean up audio with one-click enhancement that removes noise and levels voices. A text-to-speech and voice cloning feature lets creators fix a mistake by typing.

The platform includes tools for video podcasts, hosting and distribution, and AI features such as summaries and show notes. It aims to give new podcasters an all-in-one workflow without learning a traditional audio editor.

item.title: Poolside
item.description:
Poolside focuses on one domain: code. The company trains large models from scratch, using reinforcement learning where the model writes code, runs it, and learns from whether it works. The aim is models that handle real software tasks reliably.

It targets customers with strict security needs, such as defense and large enterprises, and offers deployment in their own environments. Products include a coding assistant and an agent built on its models, and the company has invested heavily in computing infrastructure.

item.title: Portkey
item.description:
Portkey sits between applications and model providers. Developers send requests to Portkey, which forwards them to the chosen provider and handles retries, fallbacks to other models, caching, and load balancing. This increases reliability and makes it easy to switch models.

The platform adds visibility and governance: logs and analytics on cost and latency, prompt management, guardrails that check inputs and outputs, and budgets and access controls for teams. It supports the Model Context Protocol and agent frameworks.

item.title: Pory
item.description:
Pory turns spreadsheets and databases into websites. A user connects an Airtable base or Google Sheet, designs pages and layouts with a visual editor, and publishes a directory, portal, or dashboard. Logins and permissions control who sees what.

It is popular for member directories, job boards, simple CRMs, and client portals. Because the data stays in the source, updating the spreadsheet updates the site.

Pory has a free tier and paid plans. Complex logic is limited compared with full app builders. Alternatives include Softr, Glide, Stacker, Noloco, and Bubble. Pory suits non-developers building front ends on Airtable or Sheets.

item.title: Prefect
item.description:
Prefect lets developers turn Python functions into reliable workflows. By adding decorators, a script becomes a flow with tasks that retry on failure, run on a schedule, and report state. Teams view runs, logs, and results in a dashboard.

It supports dynamic workflows, concurrency, and deployment to different infrastructure, from a laptop to Kubernetes. A hosted cloud service handles scheduling and observability, and the open-source server can be self-hosted. It is used for data pipelines and machine learning jobs.

item.title: Preply
item.description:
Preply matches students with tutors. Learners browse profiles, filter by language, price, and availability, book a trial lesson, and then continue with a tutor of their choice. Lessons take place on the platform’s video classroom with tools for sharing materials.

The company has added AI to support learning between lessons. Speaking practice partners simulate conversation, summaries and homework are generated from lessons, and vocabulary tools help with review. Tutors can use AI to prepare materials.

item.title: PromptLayer
item.description:
PromptLayer separates prompts from code. Teams store prompts in a registry, version them, test changes against datasets, and deploy new versions without redeploying the application. Non-engineers, such as product managers and domain experts, can edit prompts in a visual interface.

Observability features log every call with inputs, outputs, cost, and latency, and let teams search and analyze history. Evaluations compare prompt versions and models, and workflows chain steps for agents.

item.title: Publer
item.description:
Publer provides the essentials of social media planning at a modest price. Users connect accounts, build a calendar, schedule posts and recurring content, and see analytics on performance. Bulk scheduling and a library of media help manage volume.

Features include collaboration and approvals, link in bio pages, and a social inbox. The AI assistant writes captions, suggests hashtags, and repurposes content, and tools recycle evergreen posts.

Publer has a free plan with limits and paid tiers by social accounts. Alternatives include Buffer, Later, Metricool, Hootsuite, and Pallyy. Publer suits creators and small teams who want an affordable scheduler.

item.title: Qdrant
item.description:
Qdrant stores vectors, the numerical representations of text, images, or other data, and finds the closest matches quickly. Applications use it for semantic search, recommendations, and retrieval-augmented generation. Metadata filters narrow results, such as by date or category.

It is built in Rust for speed and efficiency, supports quantization to reduce memory, and scales across nodes. Hybrid search combines vector similarity with keyword-style sparse vectors. It can be self-hosted or used in the managed Qdrant Cloud.

item.title: Quantified AI
item.description:
Quantified AI helps sales reps practice before they talk to real customers. A rep enters a simulated conversation with an AI buyer that responds in real time, raises objections, and changes direction, and the system scores the performance on things like discovery, handling pushback, and messaging.

Managers use the results to see who needs coaching and track progress over time, and companies can create scenarios that mirror their own sales motions and products. Practice is available any time, which helps new hires ramp faster than relying only on role-play with colleagues.

item.title: Quantilope
item.description:
Quantilope aims to let research teams run advanced studies without waiting weeks on an agency. Researchers pick from automated methods, such as concept tests, segmentation, pricing studies, and brand tracking, set up the survey, and field it to respondents from a panel. Analysis and charts are generated as data comes in.

The platform’s AI helps design studies, suggests suitable methods, writes summaries of findings, and answers questions about the data. Because methodologies are built in, non-specialists can run studies that would normally need a statistician.

item.title: Ray
item.description:
Ray makes it easier to run Python code across many machines. A developer adds simple decorators to turn functions into distributed tasks, and Ray schedules them across a cluster. On top of this core sit libraries for data processing, training, tuning, and serving models.

It is widely used in machine learning: large model training jobs, batch inference, and reinforcement learning rely on it, and major AI labs and companies build on it. Anyscale, the company founded by its creators, offers a managed platform.

item.title: Recraft
item.description:
Recraft is aimed at designers. Besides raster images, it can produce true vector graphics, such as logos, icons, and illustrations, that remain sharp at any size and can be edited in design software. Style controls keep outputs consistent across a project.

Brand features let a team upload colors, fonts, and example images so generations follow a style. The model handles text in images well, which helps with posters and mockups. Editing tools allow changing parts of an image, removing backgrounds, and upscaling.

item.title: Reducto
item.description:
Reducto turns messy documents into clean data. A developer sends a PDF or image, and the API returns structured output that preserves layout, tables, and figures, which can feed language models or databases. It combines vision models and traditional techniques to handle difficult pages.

Applications include financial analysis, legal review, healthcare records, and RAG systems where poor parsing hurts answer quality. Options exist for extracting fields to a schema and for splitting documents by type. Enterprises can deploy it in their own environment.

item.title: Refact.ai
item.description:
Refact.ai gives developers an assistant they can control. It offers autocomplete, chat that understands the codebase, and an agent that can carry out tasks like fixing bugs, running tests, and refactoring. It plugs into popular editors.

Privacy is a key benefit: companies can run it on their own servers with open models so code never leaves their environment, or use cloud models. Fine-tuning on a codebase is available in some setups.

item.title: Reka AI
item.description:
Reka is a research lab and company founded by researchers from DeepMind, Google, and Meta. It trains models from scratch that take mixed inputs, so a user can ask questions about a video or combine audio and text. The Flash and Edge models are smaller and faster, and Core is the largest.

Products built on the models include tools for research tasks that search and reason over the web, and for analyzing video. Developers use the API, and the company has released some models openly. Efficiency is a recurring theme in its work.

item.title: Relay
item.description:
Relay.app takes the Zapier-style approach and adds two things: AI steps and humans in the loop. A workflow can trigger on an event, call an AI to summarize or draft, then pause for a teammate to approve before the next action runs. This suits tasks where full automation is risky.

Integrations connect common business tools, and a visual builder makes flows easy to design. Examples include drafting replies for review, routing leads, and preparing reports. Approvals can be done in email or Slack.

item.title: Relevance AI
item.description:
Relevance AI lets teams create agents without code. A user defines what an agent does, gives it instructions and tools such as web search, email, or a CRM, and connects knowledge sources. Several agents can be assembled into a team, with one handing work to another.

Common uses are sales development, research, support, and operations. Templates give a starting point, and a monitoring layer shows what agents did and where they need help. Integrations connect with business tools, and agents can run on triggers or schedules.

item.title: Remesh
item.description:
Remesh scales the focus group. A moderator poses questions to hundreds of participants at once, and people respond in their own words and then rate each other’s answers, so the group quickly reveals where opinions agree and differ. Responses are analyzed as they arrive.

AI clusters comments into themes, summarizes sentiment, and highlights segments by demographic. Researchers use it for message testing, employee listening, public policy input, and product research. A single session can produce depth and breadth that would take many interviews.

item.title: Respeecher
item.description:
Respeecher works through speech-to-speech conversion. A performer records a line, and the system transforms it into the voice of a target speaker, keeping the performer’s emotion and timing. This differs from text-to-speech, which generates speech from scratch and can lack nuance.

Productions have used it to recreate the voices of actors who are unavailable, age or de-age a voice, and dub into other languages while preserving a character’s sound. The company emphasizes licensing and consent from voice owners.

item.title: Revenue.io
item.description:
Revenue.io, formerly RingDNA, combines calling with conversation intelligence. During a call, it listens and surfaces prompts, such as a competitor battlecard or the right answer to a pricing objection. After the call, it transcribes, summarizes, and scores conversations against a playbook.

Managers get coaching insights and forecasting signals. The platform includes a dialer and integrates with Salesforce, so call data flows into the CRM. AI assistants draft follow-ups and update records.

item.title: Riffusion
item.description:
Riffusion started as a research demo that generated music clips by running Stable Diffusion on spectrogram images, an early sign that diffusion models could make audio. It grew into a platform where users type a prompt and get a song with vocals, and into a chat-like agent that helps produce tracks.

The brand changed to Producer.ai, and reports say it has since moved under Google’s music efforts, so product names and features may keep changing. Users should check the current site and how their saved songs and rights are handled through any transition.

item.title: Rodin
item.description:
Rodin creates 3D assets from simple inputs. A user types a description or uploads an image, and the system produces a textured 3D model that can be exported to common formats. It also offers options for controlling geometry and materials.

The output can serve as a starting point for games, animation, product visualization, and augmented reality. Quality has improved quickly in this field, but generated meshes often need cleanup of topology and textures before production use.

item.title: RoomGPT
item.description:
RoomGPT lets people visualize a space in new styles. A user uploads a photo of a living room or bedroom, chooses a theme such as modern, minimalist, or tropical, and the AI generates redesigned images that keep the room’s structure while changing furniture and decor.

Homeowners use it for inspiration before shopping or renovating, and some real estate agents use it for staging ideas. Results show style direction but do not match real products or exact dimensions.

item.title: Rossum
item.description:
Rossum reads business documents without fixed templates. Companies receive invoices in many formats, and Rossum identifies fields such as vendor, amount, and line items, validates them against rules, and sends clean data to accounting or ERP systems.

A review interface lets staff correct uncertain fields, and the system learns from corrections. Workflows handle approvals and matching with purchase orders. The company has moved to a transactional language model approach for understanding documents.

item.title: Salesflare
item.description:
Salesflare fills itself in. It connects to email, calendar, and phone, then builds contact and company profiles with conversation history, social data, and notes, so sales reps do not need to type everything. A timeline shows every interaction with a contact.

Features include pipelines, workflows, email tracking, and sequences, plus an intelligent assistant that nudges reps when a lead has gone quiet. It works with Gmail, Outlook, and a mobile app.

item.title: Sapling
item.description:
Sapling helps support and sales teams write faster and more consistently. As an agent types in the help desk or CRM, Sapling suggests completions based on past replies, fixes grammar and tone, and inserts approved snippets. This reduces typing time and variation.

Managers use quality analytics to monitor response times and consistency, and see how suggestions are used. It integrates with Zendesk, Salesforce, Intercom, and other tools, and offers an API and an AI content detector.

item.title: SeekOut
item.description:
SeekOut builds a searchable database of professionals from public profiles and sources. Recruiters filter by skills, experience, and background, find candidates for roles like engineers and scientists, and reach out with outreach sequences.

AI helps match candidates to jobs and understand skill sets, and analytics show talent pools in a region or company. Diversity filters support recruiting programs, subject to legal rules on how they are used. Products extend to internal talent management for employers.

item.title: Shortly AI
item.description:
Shortly AI was one of the early GPT-based writing tools built for fiction and long-form content. A writer types, and with a keystroke the assistant continues the text in the same voice, or offers rewrites and alternatives. It aimed to keep the writer in control of the direction.

It was used for blog posts, stories, and essays, particularly to push through slow stretches. The product emerged before general chat assistants became widely used, and those assistants now cover much of the same ground.

item.title: Slab
item.description:
Slab gives teams a clean place to write and organize internal documentation. Content is arranged in topics, and the editor emphasizes readability. Engineering, support, and operations teams use it for runbooks, handbooks, and policies.

Search is the core feature. It queries Slab content and connected tools such as Google Drive, GitHub, and Slack in one place, and the AI answers questions in natural language with links to sources. Verification features prompt owners to keep pages up to date.

item.title: Sloyd
item.description:
Sloyd takes a different approach from mesh generators. Its models are parametric, so a user can generate a chair or a sword and then adjust sliders for size, shape, and style, and get clean, game-ready geometry with proper topology. Real-time generation fits into workflows and game engines.

A library of templates and an API let developers generate assets inside their own tools and games, including at runtime. The aim is to reduce the time artists spend on common props and set dressing.

item.title: SmartRecruiters
item.description:
SmartRecruiters is an applicant tracking system built for large companies. Recruiters post jobs to many boards, receive and manage applications, collaborate with hiring managers on evaluations, schedule interviews, and extend offers, all in one workflow. A marketplace of integrations connects background checks, assessments, video interviewing, and HR systems, which suits global companies with complex hiring needs.

AI features support sourcing and screening. The platform recommends candidates from existing applicants and external pools, scores fit against job requirements, and helps with scheduling and communication. Its AI assistant can draft job descriptions and summarize candidate profiles, and analytics show the hiring funnel, time to fill, and diversity metrics. The company states it emphasizes transparency in how AI recommendations are made.

item.title: Speechmatics
item.description:
Speechmatics provides speech-to-text as a service. Developers send audio and get transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and language detection. The company emphasizes accuracy across accents and dialects, which is an area where many systems show bias.

Products include real-time transcription for live captioning and voice agents, batch processing, translation, and deployment options on premises for sensitive data. Customers include media, contact center, and healthcare companies.

Speechmatics is priced by usage. Alternatives include Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI Whisper, Gladia, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text. Speechmatics suits organizations needing accurate multilingual transcription.

item.title: Spike
item.description:
Spike presents email like a chat. Threads become conversations, which can feel faster, and a unified view combines email with notes, tasks, and calendar. Teams can discuss messages privately without forwarding.

AI helps with summaries of long threads, drafting replies, and organizing the inbox, and shared inboxes support small teams. It works with many email providers.

Spike has a free tier and paid plans. Chat-style email is a taste, and some prefer traditional layouts. Alternatives include Superhuman, Shortwave, Hey, Gmail with Gemini, and Front. Spike suits people who want a conversational inbox.

item.title: Splice
item.description:
Splice supplies the building blocks of modern production. Producers search a huge catalog of samples by genre, key, and tempo, preview them in sync with their project, and download them under a license that allows use in released music. Plugin subscriptions let users rent instruments and effects.

AI features assist with creativity. Tools suggest compatible samples, and apps generate loops and ideas. Cloud project backup and collaboration features help producers work with others.

item.title: Spring Health
item.description:
Spring Health provides employer-sponsored mental health care. Employees take an assessment, and the system recommends a path, from self-guided tools to coaching, therapy, or psychiatric care, with a care navigator to help. Providers are drawn from its network.

AI and measurement-based care play a role in matching and tracking progress. The company states that it collects outcomes data to adjust care. It serves employers, health plans, and other organizations.

Anyone in crisis should reach emergency services or a crisis line. Spring Health is sold to organizations, not directly to individuals. Alternatives include Lyra Health, Headspace Health, Talkspace, Modern Health, and Teladoc. Spring Health suits employees whose employers offer it.

item.title: Stable Audio
item.description:
Stable Audio generates sound from descriptions. A user types a prompt such as an upbeat electronic track with a driving bass line, and the model produces a piece of the requested length. It can also create sound effects and ambient textures.

The models were trained on licensed audio, which Stability emphasizes to address rights concerns. Producers and sound designers use it for sketching ideas, backing tracks, and game audio. Smaller open models can run locally.

item.title: Stablecog
item.description:
Stablecog offers image generation without the setup of running a model locally. Users enter a prompt, choose a model and settings, and receive images in seconds. The code is open, and the project is run as a community-minded service.

It appeals to hobbyists who want to try Stable Diffusion and its variants and to developers who want a reference for building their own interface. Free credits are available, with paid options for more use.

item.title: Streak
item.description:
Streak adds pipeline management to Gmail. Users create boxes for deals, candidates, or projects, move them through stages, and see all related emails, notes, and files in one place. Because it sits in the inbox, there is little context switching.

Features include mail merge, email tracking, scheduling, shared inboxes, and automations. AI helps summarize threads and draft emails. It suits small teams that already run on Google Workspace.

Streak has a free plan and paid tiers. It is tied to Gmail. Alternatives include Copper, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Close, and Attio. Streak suits small teams working from the inbox.

item.title: Submagic
item.description:
Submagic speeds up editing of talking-head clips. A creator uploads a video, the tool transcribes speech, adds styled captions that highlight words as they are spoken, and suggests emojis, sound effects, and B-roll to keep viewers engaged.

Templates provide the caption looks seen on popular social videos, and users can edit text, timing, and style. Tools for trimming silence and magic clips from longer videos add to the toolkit. Multiple languages are supported.

item.title: Sweep AI
item.description:
Sweep started as an AI junior developer on GitHub. A user described a task in an issue, and the bot read the code, planned changes, and opened a pull request. The team found it hard to reach the reliability they wanted and noticed that most AI coding attention was focused on VS Code.

They pivoted to a JetBrains plugin for IntelliJ, PyCharm, and other IDEs, offering context-aware chat, multi-file apply, and automated code review. The plugin can run in on-premises settings, which suits companies with security needs.

item.title: Tailor Brands
item.description:
Tailor Brands serves new businesses. A user enters a company name and preferences, and the AI proposes logos and a brand kit with colors and fonts, then applies it to business cards, social graphics, and a website. The goal is a complete starter identity in minutes.

The platform has added services around the brand: website building, domain, and incorporation help. Subscriptions bundle logos and tools.

Tailor Brands has a free tier to design and paid plans to download. AI logos can resemble others, and trademark checks are the user’s job. Alternatives include Looka, Canva, LogoAI, Wix Logo Maker, and hiring a designer. Tailor Brands suits small business owners starting a brand.

item.title: Tavily
item.description:
Tavily provides web search for machines. A developer sends a query and receives ranked results with cleaned content and sources, trimmed to what a language model needs, so agents can ground answers in current information. Extra endpoints extract text from pages, crawl sites, and run deeper research.

It integrates with frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex and with the Model Context Protocol, which made it a common choice for adding web access to agents. A free tier supports experimentation.

item.title: Tensor.Art
item.description:
